citation: §Appendix C (Terminology Service; Public Health Surveillance Platform; Logical Information Model Repository); Appendix F p.69 / 170 / 176 / 226 / 241–242 l.Terminology Service requirements 21 and 24; Public Health Surveillance Platform requirements 18 and 19; Logical Information Model Repository requirement 7; Appendix F p.241 L4–7 and Table F
anchorNote: placed on the block, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (high): Suggests a new Terminology Service requirement beside reqs 21 and 24; this is the TS functional-requirements table holding req 21
summary: The draft names this hazard itself: without semantic governance, "the same coded value is interpreted differently by di…
text:
The draft names this hazard itself: without semantic governance, "the same coded value is interpreted differently by different systems, or systems maintain inconsistent local copies of code systems, making aggregation and comparison unreliable" (p.69).

The contract the requirements then write is asymmetric. Two components are Required to consume a capability the provider is only advised to offer. Public Health Surveillance Platform requirement 18 is Required: the platform "shall subscribe to update notifications from the Terminology Service to ensure surveillance case definitions and reporting forms remain aligned with current terminology versions as international standards evolve" (p.226). Logical Information Model Repository requirement 7 is Required on the same pattern (p.176). The corresponding provider capability, requirement 21, by which a consuming system learns that an artefact was "updated, deprecated, or retired", is Recommended (p.170).

The nearest thing the draft does require is Public Health Surveillance Platform requirement 19 (p.226, Required), which monitors the "timeliness, completeness, and quality of surveillance data submissions" with alerts on threshold breach. That is a check on the volume, timeliness and quality of submissions. Its thresholds are set nationally, so whether the silent absence of one newly notifiable condition registers depends on how finely they are configured. Nothing in the requirement obliges that granularity, and nothing in it requires the platform to establish that a particular consumer has received a particular published change. A detection that depends on how an implementer happens to configure a threshold is not the same as a requirement that the state be demonstrable. Appendix F carries many of the enabling capabilities but is "illustrative reference material rather than a specification" (p.241). Gap detection, replay, resynchronisation, omission, cursor, sequence number, manifest and checksum return no occurrences anywhere in the draft.

The reasoning, a worked case and the measurement proposal are set out in the companion paper attached to this submission.
suggestion:
Add a Required, transport-neutral requirement to the Terminology Service alongside requirements 21 and 24. Proposed wording:

"The TS shall provide a means by which a consuming system can obtain a complete and explicitly identified copy of the terminology content it depends on, determine whether that copy is a release currently applicable to its context, and detect and recover from a change that has not reached it. The means is not prescribed: an application programming interface, a subscription, a periodic release package, syndication or a bulk export may each satisfy this requirement, and a country distributing by release package requires no change-stream capability."

Make the obligation reciprocal: where a component is Required to subscribe, as the surveillance platform and the information-model repository are, the Terminology Service should be Required to provide the mechanism they are Required to use. And extend terminology conformance testing across the producer–consumer boundary rather than against the service alone, with tests appropriate to each route: for replacement delivery, that a consumer can take a fresh complete copy and verify its identity and completeness against the published package identity; for incremental delivery, that omission and duplication are detected, that a recorded position can be resumed from, and that an unserviceable position produces an explicit condition with a route to a complete copy rather than a silent resumption.
reviewer: Vsevolod Shabad, University of Liverpool, United Kingdom

citation: §Appendix C (Terminology Service; Lifelong Health Record) / 3.5 p.159 / 167 / 168 / 169 / 170 l.Terminology Service requirement 3 (TSF-3, p.167), requirement 8 (TSF-4, p.168) and requirement 13 (TSWF-3, p.169); Lifelong Health Record requirement 3 (SHRF-7, p.159); p.170 L147–151
anchorNote: quotation found in the text
summary: The draft is deliberate about versioning at the source. Requirement 3 requires the Terminology Service to "maintain ful…
text:
The draft is deliberate about versioning at the source. Requirement 3 requires the Terminology Service to "maintain full version history of code systems, supporting concurrent active versions, defined lifecycle states (draft, active, deprecated, retired), and consumer-specified version requests", and explains the choice: "DPI-H elevates this to Required where OpenHIE treats it as a Recommendation; versioning is essential for a governance-grade national terminology service to honour backwards compatibility obligations" (p.167). Requirement 8 does the same for value sets, and the summary of departures from OpenHIE confirms it (p.170, L147–151).

What is not stated is what version and temporal context a consuming system must retain with coded data when interpretation is version-dependent. A service able to reconstruct every release does not help a historical clinical record that carries a bare code, and therefore does not identify which meaning, which value-set membership, which display or which mapping applied when the record was created.

The record side of the draft shows how close it already is. The Lifelong Health Record must "record and version all updates to clinical data; records shall never be deleted, only marked as such; no previous version of a record shall be overwritten; all prior versions shall remain retrievable" (requirement 3, SHRF-7, p.159, Required). That is immutability of the record. It is not immutability of the record's interpretation: every prior version of the entry is retrievable, and the requirement does not ensure that any of them carries, or can resolve, the code-system version, expansion or map that governed its meaning when it was written.

An effective date alone would not close this. Publication time, the period during which an artefact is approved for use, the version a consumer actually applied, and the time a notification was delivered are four different facts, and reconstructing a past interpretation needs more than one of them. The service can already do the work. Requirement 13 obliges the Terminology Service to "expand value sets into the explicit list of concepts they contain at a given point in time, accounting for the version of the underlying code systems and the expansion parameters supplied by the consumer" (p.169, Required). Reconstructing a past reading is therefore an available operation – but only to a caller who still holds the parameters it needs, and nothing requires the record to retain them.
suggestion:
Add a Required temporal-provenance requirement: published code systems, value sets and concept maps carry stable identifiers, explicit business versions, release dates and, where applicable, effective periods, and a published expansion carries its own identifier, the time at which it was produced, and the parameters and underlying code-system versions used to produce it – requirement 13 already names those inputs; and, where clinical or operational interpretation depends on a terminology release or a governing profile, the record preserves or can resolve the code-system version together with the identifiers, versions and temporal context of the profile, value-set expansion or map on which that interpretation depended. Stating the condition this way keeps the requirement bounded: it does not ask every coded value to carry an expansion version regardless of context, and it does not disturb the concurrent active versions the draft permits. A change should not silently assign a materially different meaning to an existing versionless identifier, but should create an explicitly distinguishable version or identifier while preserving access to the prior meaning.

The architecture is standards-neutral and need not name FHIR elements, but the semantic equivalents are what this requires: a business version, a revision date and an effective period on each of CodeSystem, ValueSet and ConceptMap; for an expansion, its own identifier with the timestamp and the parameters and underlying code-system versions that produced it; and Coding.version travelling with the coded value wherever interpretation is version-dependent. FHIR's own guidance against changing the meaning of an existing code is the practice being asked for. Extend conformance testing to include retrospective interpretation of a record created under a prior active version.
reviewer: Vsevolod Shabad, University of Liverpool, United Kingdom

citation: §Appendix C (Health Facility Registry; Product Registry; Supplier Registry) p.132 / 149 / 193 / 196 l.Health Facility Registry requirement 22; Product Registry requirement 16 and note at p.149 L481–483; Supplier Registry p.193 L93 and requirement 18
anchorNote: quotation found in the text
summary: The note beneath the Product Registry table states that "Cross-cutting requirements (audit logging, subscription and no…
text:
The note beneath the Product Registry table states that "Cross-cutting requirements (audit logging, subscription and notification, performance and availability) apply consistently across all registry components" (p.149, L481–483), and the Supplier Registry is described as completing "the three-pillar master data foundation for health supply chain operations alongside the Product Registry and the Health Facility Registry" (p.193, L93).

Two of those three pillars are required to be designed for high availability: the Product Registry, on the ground that supply-chain systems at all levels depend on product master data for operational transactions (p.149, requirement 16), and the Health Facility Registry, because facility identity and location data are referenced across supply chain, clinical, financial and surveillance domains (p.132, requirement 22). The Supplier Registry alone is required to be designed for "adequate availability" – the only occurrence of that phrase in the document – on closely parallel reasoning, adding regulatory verification (p.196, requirement 18). Where the draft grades a component lower elsewhere it gives its reason: the Logical Information Model Repository is set at "sufficient reliability and performance" because design-time access is typically less latency-sensitive (p.178, requirement 17). No reason is given here.

The difference may be intentional. But neither "high" nor "adequate" defines a testable service level, and recovery objectives are a different measure: the Lifelong Health Record's "defined recovery time and recovery point objectives" (p.162, requirement 21) address recovery from failure, not availability, response time, or how stale a cached copy may become.
suggestion: Either align the Supplier Registry with the other two pillars at high availability, or state the architectural reason for the lower grade as explicitly as the Logical Information Model Repository's reason is stated. In either case, require countries to define measurable service objectives appropriate to the use case, covering availability, response time, maximum acceptable staleness where cached reference data is used, and recovery time and recovery point objectives. Section 3.6.5 asks that requirements be made testable so vendor claims can be validated in procurement; a grade expressed as an adjective cannot be.
reviewer: Vsevolod Shabad, University of Liverpool, United Kingdom

changeSets.title: Define service levels and operational readiness for shared components

anchorNote: p.35–36 / 78 / 98 l.Principle IX L392–427; 3.6.5 L955–959; 4.3.5 L400–401 read as the printed page; section 3.6.5 does NOT agree
summary: Principle IX makes trust and security architectural properties while appropriately leaving "the specific controls, conf…
text:
Principle IX makes trust and security architectural properties while appropriately leaving "the specific controls, configurations, and operational practices" to implementation and national security policy (L426–427). The procurement and conformance material nevertheless supplies no common supplier-assurance baseline against which a country can evaluate how a DPI-H software component was built and how it will be maintained. Section 3.6.5 asks that requirements be testable "so that countries can validate conformance – including the claims of vendors – before and during procurement" (L955–959), and section 4.3.5 asks countries to "establish minimum conformance requirements for each DPI-H component and define the testing mechanisms through which conformance is assessed" (L400–401) – but both concern conformance to interoperability and information-model profiles. Appendix C commonly requires access control and audit logging, which are properties of the running system.

Across the draft there is no occurrence of software bill of materials, vulnerability, secure development, penetration testing or end-of-support. A component can therefore satisfy its information-model and access-control requirements without the guidance asking the supplier to identify its material dependencies, state how long the version will be supported, provide a route for reporting a vulnerability, or show how a security defect reaches deployed installations as a trusted update. This is a completeness gap in the common architecture rather than a request for WHO to prescribe a national control framework, and it sits on a different axis from interoperability conformance.
suggestion:
Add a risk-proportionate supplier software-assurance baseline to Principle IX, and cross-reference it from the procurement and conformance guidance rather than placing it inside section 4.3.5, which addresses interoperability profiles. The baseline should ask for evidence covering: supported versions and end-of-support dates; material third-party dependencies through a software bill of materials or equivalent inventory; a coordinated vulnerability-disclosure route; triage and remediation expectations proportionate to severity and clinical criticality; an authenticated mechanism for delivering security updates to deployed installations; and a secure development and maintenance lifecycle.

IEC 81001-5-1 may be referenced for health-software lifecycle activities and NIST SP 800-218 for outcome-based secure-development practices and purchaser-supplier communication. They are not interchangeable and neither should be presented as a mandatory control set: IEC 81001-5-1 governs lifecycle activities and expressly excludes the content of accompanying documentation, so citing it does not by itself procure a dependency inventory. Conformance should assess declared evidence and lifecycle commitments rather than possession of a certificate.
reviewer: Vsevolod Shabad, University of Liverpool, United Kingdom

anchorNote: p.99 l.L451–453 ("Standards conformance" bullet) read as the printed page; section 4.4.2 agrees
summary: The progress dimensions are well chosen, but the standards-conformance dimension measures a property of deployment rath…
text: The progress dimensions are well chosen, but the standards-conformance dimension measures a property of deployment rather than a property of present state. It asks whether components "conform to open standards, expose standard APIs, and use governed terminology and data models" (p.99, L451–453). A system can satisfy all three while holding a superseded version of the terminology it uses: it conforms, it exposes the API, and it uses the governed artefact – just not the release currently applicable to it. That is the failure raised in comment 1, and it is invisible to this indicator as written.
suggestion:
Extend the "Standards conformance" bullet with a currency clause. Proposed wording, to be appended to the existing bullet:

"...and whether deployed components can demonstrate that they hold a version of the governed terminology and data models that is currently applicable to their context."
reviewer: Vsevolod Shabad, University of Liverpool, United Kingdom

text: The document never explicitly resolves where the Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) sits in the governance hierarchy. Section 3.4.3 says strategic governance "does not manage operations; it creates the mandate" (lines 293–294). Section 3.4.4 says operational governance includes "interoperability and semantic governance… through the Semantic Governance Infrastructure described in 3.4.5" (lines 355–358), which places SGI under operational governance. But Section 3.4.5 then describes SGI as "cross-cutting" and "not a component of any single registry" (lines 414–416) whose scope spans "global, national and local content" (lines 412–413) — work that sounds strategic (national standards alignment, clinical reality reflection). The reader is left uncertain: Is SGI an operational function executing strategic policy? A strategic function with operational mechanics? Or a third layer between the two?
suggestion: State explicitly in 3.4.5 whether SGI decisions route through operational governance alone, strategic governance alone, or both depending on decision type, and adjust the 3.4.4 bullet to reflect that SGI is not solely an operational output.

suggestion: A referance architecture serves as a technology-independent framework that delineates the fundamental components, interconnections and design principles of technical ecosystem, enabling organisations to avoid beginning from scratch. Utilising recognised enterprise architectural methodologies, it acts as a definitive referance that directs the creation of more tailored architectures and solutions, while providing an organised framework of reusable components. Its significance resides in providing various stakeholders with a unified framework - a collective terminology and organisational structure that harmonises decisions, minimises redundancy and facilitates the integration and sustainability of application components. In the context of health, where services are provided through numerous programs, institutions and tiers of care, this holds particular significance. A reference architecture offers nations a unified method to convert broad health policy objectives into digital frameworks taht are interoperable, manageable, and tailored to their specific circumstances.

suggestion: The G20 characterised DPI as a collection of collaborative digital infrastructures that must be secure and interoperable, constructed on open standards and specifications to ensure equitable access to public and/or private services at a societal level, governed by relevant legal frameworks and enabling regulations to promote development, inclusion, innovation, trust and competition, while upholding human rights and fundamental freedoms. Collectively, these criteria delineate essential attributes of DPI: it functions as a communal infrastructure at a society level, and its value arises not from an individual system but from its open, interoperable basis that enables both public and private entities to innovate. The G20 acknowledges that Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) is a dynamic notion, not confined to systems with particular features, and may be customised to fit the unique situations of many nations, often referred to by diverse terminology. This establishes the foundation for expressing a health-centric interpretation of DPI, tailored to the requirements of the health sector while aligning with the broad agreement. This health-specific digital public infrastructure is derived from a comprehensive cross-sectoral understanding.

text: The first aspect is focused on collective resources. DPI-H is not a compilation of specialised tools or service-specific apps; rather, it is an infrastructure that is communal, reusable and accessible to all stakeholders in the health system, eliminating the need for each to develop comparable capablilities independently. The second pertains to the connection between DPI-H and fundamental DPI. DPI-H does not aim to duplicate the offerings of foundational DPI; instead, it enhances and supplements them with the specialised funstionalities necessary for the health sector that general-purpose DPI cannot fulfil. Where basic DPI is present and available, DPI-H expands upon it. In instances where it falls short, DPI-H delivers the crucial functionalities required for the health system to operate, while maintaining an architechturally flexible framework for integration as the larger digital ecosystem evolves.

text: This joint submission synthesises two critical reviews written independently and without sight of each other (a semantics-and-standards review and an integrated-care review; their convergence is documented in a separate comparison). Both commend the same strengths: the Semantic Governance Infrastructure (meaning as a permanently governed asset — institutions first, tools second); the outcome-defined Lifelong Health Record; the draft's realism (no country starts from zero; conformance as a graded model); and Chapter 5's sober treatment of AI. Both also identify the same missing piece: the draft's own definition of interoperability ends with 'use the exchanged information to execute functions effectively', yet nowhere is that effective use designed, supported or measured. Conformance verifies systems and transactions, never whether the receiving human understood the information and acted appropriately (the 'last mile'). Likewise 'capture once, use many times' silently assumes reuse is free, while in practice information must be transformed to each receiver's role and context ('informational metamorphosis') — a transformation that is neither designed nor governed. Comments 2–15 below make this actionable; that two unconnected critiques converge on the same point is itself evidence the gap is real.
suggestion: Extend the draft's own logic — govern meaning, define by outcome, verify by testing — to the point of action, per the specific proposals in comments 2–15.
reviewer: Gerard Freriks and Angelo Rossi-Mori, Gerard Freriks is Affilated with CEN and ISO, Netherlands / Europe

text: The architecture governs the stewardship of information models (SGI, LIMR) but does not standardise how models are made. Current artefact standards allow too many degrees of freedom: the same clinical concept can be modelled in many valid but incompatible ways, so two fully conformant implementations may still diverge semantically. A related, unnamed risk is the boundary problem: qualifiers, modifiers and localisations can be expressed in either the terminology or the information model, and this overlap breeds divergence.
suggestion: Require (in §3.4.5 and Appendix C) that artefacts in the LIMR be produced with a declared, uniform modelling method — one generic semantic pattern from which artefacts are derived by specialisation, with mandatory context (what, where, when, who, how, why) at capture — and test that meaning survives its application. The emerging CEN/ISO 13606 part 3 (SIAMM) work is one standards-track candidate; the requirement itself should remain method-neutral. Explicitly name — and assign governance responsibility for — the boundary problem between coding systems and information models.
reviewer: Gerard Freriks and Angelo Rossi-Mori, Gerard Freriks is Affilated with CEN and ISO, Netherlands / Europe

text: The REDDHI open standards list (line 148) and surrounding text reference SNOMED CT, ICD-11, and LOINC as a group without articulating that these are complementary, not interchangeable, standards. Each occupies a distinct clinical domain: SNOMED CT covers clinical concepts and findings; ICD-11-MMS supports morbidity/mortality classification and reimbursement; LOINC standardises laboratory and clinical observation identifiers. A country implementing only one of these three would produce a functionally incomplete Terminology Service. The current grouping may lead national programmes to conclude that any single standard satisfies the architectural requirement.
suggestion: Add a clarifying sentence following the open standards list: "These standards are complementary rather than interchangeable: SNOMED CT provides clinical concept and procedural coverage; ICD-11 MMS supports mortality and morbidity classification; LOINC provides universal identifiers for laboratory tests and clinical observations. A complete national Terminology Service typically requires all three, operating together."

WHO and ITU are invited to establish a formal Technical Advisory Group, comprising SNOMED International and fellow SDOs such as Regenstrief Institute for LOINC, HL7 International, and WHO, to develop SGI implementation guidance for national programmes."

text: Line 814 and Table 3.5 enumerate SNOMED CT (and SNOMED GPS), ICD-11, and LOINC as required terminology standards. The document is silent on cross-maps between these standards, specifically the SNOMED CT to ICD-11 MMS map and the SNOMED CT-LOINC alignment. These cross-maps are operationally essential: a country using SNOMED CT for clinical data capture must map to ICD-11 MMS for administrative and statistical reporting. Without authoritative cross-maps, countries will build their own divergent, unmaintained mappings or fail to meet both requirements simultaneously. Historically, SNOMED International and WHO have collaborated on an official SNOMED CT-ICD 10 map; SNOMED International and Regenstrief collaborate on SNOMED CT-LOINC alignment via the LOINC Ontology. These resources are precisely what implementing countries will need.
suggestion: We suggest the authors add to section 3.4.5 or Table 3.5: "Cross-maps between SNOMED CT, ICD-11 MMS, and LOINC are a required component of a functional national Terminology Service, not an optional enhancement. WHO and ITU should commission a joint Mapping Governance White Paper, co-authored with SNOMED International, WHO's ICD-11 programme, and Regenstrief Institute, providing countries with authoritative guidance on deploying and maintaining cross-terminology maps within their national SGI. Official SNOMED CT-ICD 10 maps are available from SNOMED International; and the LOINC Ontology from Regenstrief and SNOMED International jointly."
reviewer: Don Sweete, SNOMED International, Global (international not-for-profit SDO)

suggestion: We suggest to add to Section 3.7.2 or 3.7.3: "For Terminology Service components, the HL7 FHIR Terminology Service specification (R4/R5, http://hl7.org/fhir/terminology-service.html) provides a ready-made, machine-testable conformance baseline. text: The SGI section addresses terminology governance within a country but does not address the international release cycle dimension: national SGI bodies must receive, validate, localise, and distribute versioned terminology releases from international SDOs on defined schedules (SNOMED CT: monthly; LOINC: biannual; ICD-11: annual). The governance of this international-to-national terminology flow (requests for change, maintenance, version management, localisation authority, and release validation), is entirely absent from the current text. Without this, countries will develop ad-hoc processes that diverge from authoritative international releases.
suggestion:
Add paragraph: "National SGI bodies are responsible for receiving, validating, and distributing versioned releases from international terminology organisations on their published schedules. Countries should establish formal version management processes aligned to the release cycles of each terminology. SNOMED International's NRC Release Pipeline provides a reference model for national SNOMED CT release management. Countries are encouraged to participate in SDO governance processes to receive advance notice of content changes and contribute to international content development." 

Additionally, we encourage the WHO/ITU to work directly with SNOMED Interantional, and to establish a formal Technical Advisory Group, comprising SNOMED International and fellow SDOs such as Regenstrief Institute for LOINC, HL7 International, and WHO, to develop SGI implementation guidance for national programmes. The SNOMED International NRC model is highlighted throughout the document as a tried and true model, having our organization in the partnership will help to faciliate this framework beyond theory and into working practice.
reviewer: Don Sweete, SNOMED International, Global (international not-for-profit SDO)

anchorNote: quotation found in the text
summary: SNOMED CT definition is too narrow. The DPI-H Glossary defines SNOMED CT as "a structured clinical terminology standard…
text: SNOMED CT definition is too narrow. The DPI-H Glossary defines SNOMED CT as "a structured clinical terminology standard for use in electronic health records." This is materially incomplete. SNOMED CT is used for clinical decision support, population health analytics, disease surveillance, research and registry data, AI/ML model training, and interoperability across virtually every digital health domain, not only EHRs. Defining it as an EHR tool understates its architectural relevance to the very components DPI-H describes: the CDSE, HMIS, PHSP, and Terminology Service all depend on SNOMED CT in ways that go beyond EHR coding.
suggestion: We suggest a change to the following definition: "SNOMED CT: a comprehensive, multilingual clinical terminology providing a structured, hierarchical representation of clinical concepts including clinical findings, procedures, body structures, and observable entities, used for data capture, clinical decision support, population health analytics, disease surveillance, and research across digital health systems."
reviewer: Don Sweete, SNOMED International, Global (international not-for-profit SDO)

anchorNote: quotation found in the text
summary: SNOMED CT Global Patient Set (GPS) definition ("a list of basic clinical terms") is inaccurate in two respects. First, …
text: SNOMED CT Global Patient Set (GPS) definition ("a list of basic clinical terms") is inaccurate in two respects. First, "basic" is wrong: the GPS is a curated, clinically meaningful subset of the SNOMED CT International Edition, providing broad coverage of the most clinically relevant concepts across findings, procedures, medications, and other domains. Second, the word "basic" may actively deter adoption by implying inadequacy for serious clinical use, which is the opposite of the document's intent. The definition also omits the GPS's most important policy feature: it is freely available to all countries without any SNOMED International membership requirement or fee. This is the primary access pathway for LMIC implementations and should be stated plainly in the Glossary.
suggestion: We suggest the following change: "SNOMED CT Global Patient Set (GPS): a curated subset of the SNOMED CT International Edition, providing broad coverage of clinically essential concepts across findings, procedures, and related domains. The GPS is freely available to all countries at no charge, with no membership requirement, providing an immediate zero-cost access pathway for national terminology services in any country."
reviewer: Don Sweete, SNOMED International, Global (international not-for-profit SDO)

citation: §3.6.4 p.87–88 l.line 942 and Appendix C Terminology Service, §1
anchorNote: placed on the block, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (high): Cites 3.6.4 line 942 on IPS; this block (l.941-951) names the IPS
summary: Section 3.6.4 recommends the International Patient Summary (IPS) as the cross-border exchange standard for the minimum …
text:
Section 3.6.4 recommends the International Patient Summary (IPS) as the cross-border exchange standard for the minimum health data set. The IPS is named without noting that SNOMED CT is the primary clinical terminology binding in the IPS specification. The HL7 FHIR IPS Implementation Guide binds clinical findings, procedures, and allergies to SNOMED CT value sets. Countries implementing IPS conformance will therefore require SNOMED CT (or GPS) for clinical coding regardless of whether the Terminology Service section makes that explicit.

This is a direct, normative dependency that should be stated. Omitting it allows a country to read §3.6.4 and the Terminology Service component description independently, without understanding that IPS conformance effectively mandates SNOMED CT.
suggestion: Suggested addition to §3.6.4: "The IPS HL7 FHIR Implementation Guide binds key clinical elements, including problems, allergies, and procedure, to SNOMED CT value sets. Countries implementing IPS-conformant data exchange should plan for SNOMED CT (or SNOMED CT GPS for non-member countries) as the clinical terminology underpinning their IPS profiles."
reviewer: Don Sweete, SNOMED International, Global (international not-for-profit SDO)

changeSets.title: Explain the complementary roles of SNOMED CT, ICD-11 and LOINC

anchorNote: Table 3.5 as cited
summary: Chapter 5 correctly identifies governed terminology as essential infrastructure for AI-ready health data (p. 115: "term…
text:
Chapter 5 correctly identifies governed terminology as essential infrastructure for AI-ready health data (p. 115: "terminology services, which provide the semantic consistency that allows an algorithm to operate on data that means the same thing across the systems that produced it"). However, SNOMED CT is ommitted, despite SNOMED CT named in §3.4.5, and Table 3.5, as the required clinical terminology throughout the rest of the document.

Additionally, p. 116 introduces the concept of AI models calling authoritative services through shared interfaces (explicitly mentioning the Model Context Protocol), describing exactly the kind of deterministic, governed reference services that SNOMED International's Snowstorm FHIR Terminology Server and SNOMED CT FHIR API provide. These are not mentioned.

SNOMED CT's hierarchical, computable structure (including ability for post-coordinated expressions, direct attribute relationships, and transitive closure), makes it uniquely suited for ML training, NLP named entity recognition, and AI reasoning.
suggestion: Suggested addition to §5.2: "For clinical data, the governed terminology standard that delivers semantic consistency across AI training and inference is SNOMED CT, the same terminology required for the Terminology Service component described in Section 3.4.5. Its hierarchical and computable structure, which captures relationships between clinical concepts, allows AI models to generalise across equivalent clinical expressions rather than treating each code as an isolated label. The SNOMED CT GPS provides this foundation to non-member countries without cost. SNOMED International's open-source Snowstorm server implements the HL7 FHIR Terminology Service specification and is available as an authoritative, machine-callable service for AI and analytical applications."
reviewer: Don Sweete, SNOMED International, Global (international not-for-profit SDO)

changeSets.title: Broaden the foundations listed as AI enablers in 5.2

anchorNote: quotation found in the text
summary: Issue: Requirement 23 ("Federation with international sources") which covers synchronisation with content published by …
text:
Issue: Requirement 23 ("Federation with international sources") which covers synchronisation with content published by international terminology authorities including SNOMED International, WHO-FIC, and Regenstrief, is classified as Recommended, not Required. This means a national Terminology Service can achieve full DPI-H conformance without establishing any formal connection to international SDOs for terminology updates.

This is a serious structural deficiency. SNOMED CT, ICD-11, and LOINC all publish versioned releases on defined cycles (SNOMED CT: monthly; ICD-11: annual; LOINC: biannual). A national Terminology Service that does not federate with these sources will progressively diverge from authoritative international content, producing the exact semantic fragmentation that the SGI concept is designed to prevent. The classification as Recommended effectively makes international alignment optional which contradicts the document's stated purpose and the intent of §3.4.5.

Elevating this requirement to Required would be consistent with: (a) the document's own statement that the TS must manage the "lifecycle of terminologies from international adoption through national extension to local use" (p. 174); (b) the SGI governance notes in §3.4.5; and (c) the international release cycle governance comment already submitted in the formal matrix (Comment #8).
suggestion: Suggested revision: Elevate Requirement 23 from Recommended to Required. Add: "Without active federation with international terminology authorities, national Terminology Services will diverge from authoritative content releases, undermining the semantic comparability DPI-H is designed to achieve. Federation with SNOMED International (for SNOMED CT/GPS), WHO-FIC (for ICD-11), and Regenstrief (for LOINC) is therefore a conformance requirement, not an optional enhancement."
reviewer: Don Sweete, SNOMED International, Global (international not-for-profit SDO)

Issue: The country implementation examples contain two omissions relevant to SNOMED CT:

Australia (p. 241–242): Described as illustrating "Terminology Service" but the text does not mention that Australia is a SNOMED International Member country with a national SNOMED CT release (the Australian Clinical Terminology, maintained by the Australian Digital Health Agency). The example focuses on Ontoserver (correctly cited in footnote 85) but omits the national SNOMED CT governance programme that makes Ontoserver useful. For a document designed to encourage other countries to adopt national terminology services, the failure to explicitly name SNOMED CT as what Australia's national TS hosts is remissed.

Denmark (p. 242): Denmark's example focuses only on sundhed.dk (the patient health portal) and is categorised as illustrating only "LHR." Denmark is one of the founding Members of SNOMED International with an active national SNOMED CT governance programme (NRC) and a national extension, none of which is mentioned. Denmark is frequently cited as an advanced example of national SNOMED CT governance and would strengthen the document's case for the SGI model.
suggestion:
Suggested addition to Australia example: "Australia operates a national SNOMED CT programme, producing and maintaining the National Clinical Terminology Service (NCTS), run by the Australian Digital Health Agency. This is a national extension of the SNOMED CT International Edition governed by the Australian Digital Health Agency, which is hosted in Ontoserver and distributed to point-of-care systems across the country."

Suggested addition to Denmark: Add Terminology Service to Denmark's illustrated components and note: "Denmark operates a national SNOMED CT governance programme as a SNOMED International Member, providing a national extension of SNOMED CT that supports coded data capture across the Danish health system."

citation: §1.4 DPI-H Principles — Autonomy and Sovereignty p.21 l.412-416
anchorNote: p.21 l.412-416 read as the printed page; section 1.4 agrees
summary: The principle states that countries 'should not be dependent on actors outside their jurisdiction for the continued ope…
text: The principle states that countries 'should not be dependent on actors outside their jurisdiction for the continued operation or evolution of their core digital health infrastructure'. Artificial intelligence introduces a form of cross-jurisdictional dependency that the guidance does not name. A country may own every registry, exchange layer and record described in this architecture and still have every clinical decision-support inference executed on a model hosted in another jurisdiction, under that jurisdiction's export controls, and subject to a supplier's unilateral pricing and deprecation decisions. That is the dependency this principle forbids, arriving through a door the architecture leaves undescribed. The distinction that matters architecturally is not whether AI is used but whether the model can be executed within the country's own infrastructure.
suggestion: Extend the Autonomy and Sovereignty principle with a sentence to the effect: 'Where artificial intelligence forms part of a health capability, the architecture should preserve the option of in-jurisdiction inference — that is, models whose weights can be hosted and operated on national infrastructure. Dependence on a remotely hosted model that cannot be substituted or relocated is a sovereignty risk of the same class as dependence on a foreign-operated registry, and should be assessed as such.'

changeSets.title: Define 'sovereign models' and realistic AI hosting options

citation: §2.3 Design Principles — VI. Local Capacity p.33-34 l.304-322
anchorNote: p.33-34 l.304-322 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees
summary: The principle already favours 'widely supported, well-documented technologies over specialised or closed technologies w…
text: The principle already favours 'widely supported, well-documented technologies over specialised or closed technologies whose inner workings are not visible to the teams expected to run them', and states that an architecture a country cannot understand, operate and evolve with its own people is not genuinely owned by it. A model available only as a remote API is precisely a closed technology whose inner workings are not visible to the team expected to run it. The guidance makes the argument for software but does not extend it to models, which is where the argument is now most consequential.
suggestion: Add to Principle VI a clause noting that the same test applies to model artefacts: where an AI capability is adopted, preference should be given to models that in-country teams can host, inspect, evaluate and substitute, rather than models accessible only as an external service.

sectionTitle: What REDDHI is and its foundational core
citation: §2.2 REDDHI — Table 2.2, 'Longitudinal health records, with provenance and attribution' p.28 l.141 (Table 2.2)
anchorNote: Table 2.2 as cited
summary: Provenance is currently defined by the Client, Health Facility and Health Workforce registries — that is, by which pers…
text: Provenance is currently defined by the Client, Health Facility and Health Workforce registries — that is, by which person, which place and which worker. Once AI-drafted clinical content can enter a record, a third dimension is required: whether an entry was machine-generated or machine-drafted, by which system and version, and which human clinician reviewed and attested it. Without this, a Lifelong Health Record silently mixes human-authored and machine-drafted content and no subsequent audit, liability determination, quality review or model evaluation can separate them. This cannot be retrofitted: if the record structure does not carry the distinction from the outset, the historical record is permanently ambiguous. Because it concerns the foundational shared data layer rather than any point-of-service application, it belongs in this architecture and not in procurement guidance.
suggestion: Add to the provenance row of Table 2.2, and to the Lifelong Health Record component description, a requirement that record entries carry machine-generated content indicators: the authoring system and version, whether the content was machine-drafted, and the identity of the human clinician who reviewed and attested it. HL7 FHIR Provenance already supports the necessary structure, so this is a conformance expectation rather than a new component.

changeSets.title: Preserve the provenance and status of AI-generated information

anchorNote: p.34 l.325-343 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees

text: The equity principle addresses connectivity, infrastructure and institutional capacity, and requires that the architecture 'degrade gracefully rather than exclude'. Language is absent from it. In a substantial share of the settings this guidance addresses — refugee and displacement contexts, migrant populations, multilingual states, and rural populations served by clinicians trained in a national or colonial language — the patient and the clinician do not share a fluent language. This is not a user-interface localisation matter. History taken across a language barrier is systematically less complete and less accurate, and that deficit propagates directly into the registries and longitudinal records this architecture exists to make trustworthy. Language is therefore a data-quality property of the architecture, not a presentation-layer concern.
suggestion: Add language to the equity design decisions, along the lines of: 'The architecture should not assume that the person and the health worker share a language. Where they do not, the capability to capture history in the person's own language and render it into the clinical record in the working language of the health system is a data-quality requirement, not a presentation concern, and should be treated as such in conformance expectations for systems that write to the shared record.'

text: The draft uses “minimum”, “core”, “foundational core”, “shared”, “minimum viable foundation”, “canonical minimum data set” and “minimum conformance” for different kinds of concepts. These can refer to implementation feasibility, architectural centrality, shared reuse, mandatory data content or semantic necessity, but the distinctions are not defined. suggestion: Add a short terminology box distinguishing: (a) minimum implementation baseline; (b) core capability or component; (c) shared core intended for reuse across programmes or systems; (d) minimum semantic core- the least meaning and relationships that must not be lost; (e) bounded core with inclusion, exclusion and governance rules; and (f) extensible framework allowing controlled national, professional and local extensions. text: The draft correctly warns that an authoritative-looking answer may be difficult to distinguish from an unfounded one. This is a factuality-versus-fluency problem, a clear, coherent and confident output is not evidence that it is accurate, complete or supported. The architecture does not yet specify how the epistemic status of generated or inferred information should be represented and preserved.
suggestion: Require systems to distinguish visibly between a directly observed/measured data; professionally asserted or verified information; deterministically calculated information; probabilistically inferred information; and AI-generated narrative or synthesis. Do not treat fluency or a confidence score alone as proof of factuality.

citation: §3.5.3 (Figure 3.5) p.66 l.622-631; also Appendix C p. 118 line 179, Principle III (p. 32, lines 245-255) and Principle IX (p. 36, lines 415-418)
anchorNote: p.66 l.622-631; also Appendix C p. 118 line 179, Principle III (p. 32, lines 245-255) and Principle IX (p. 36, lines 415-418) read as the printed page; section 3.5.3 agrees
summary: The architecture is federated at the data layer: Principle III warns that centralised mediators create single points of…
text: The architecture is federated at the data layer: Principle III warns that centralised mediators create single points of failure and concentrations of control. Trust is then assigned wholesale to the layer beneath. Figure 3.5 places National Trust Services, itemised as PKI, digital signatures, verifiable credentials, CA and GDHCN, in the foundational DPI layer, and Appendix C states the position plainly: the Client Registry may consume PKI services, 'but PKI is a foundational DPI component that sits outside the health sector'. The result is an asymmetry of specification. Each of the twelve components in Appendix C receives functional requirements carrying a SHALL, SHOULD or MAY status. The trust services on which all twelve depend receive one box in a figure and no requirements whatever. A ministry adopting this guidance can test whether its Health Workforce Registry conforms, but has nothing against which to test the national trust service that the registry's credentials rest on, and no statement of what to require if it must procure, inherit or build one.
suggestion: State the properties a foundational trust service must exhibit to carry health-sector use, expressed as requirements on the interface between DPI-H and DPI-F, even though the implementation sits outside the health sector. At minimum: containment of compromise as Principle IX already requires; a defined key lifecycle that includes recovery and not only revocation; verifiability where connectivity is intermittent; delegation below national-authority level, so that an institution or a practitioner can be authenticated and not only an authority; and algorithm agility. Where an inherited national PKI cannot exhibit these properties, architectures built on self-certifying identifiers with verifiable key event logs (the Trust over IP KERI specification family, used as the basis of GLEIF's verifiable LEI and codified by ISO in ISO 17442-3:2024) satisfy several of them structurally and are worth naming as an admissible route. Their open questions belong in the same sentence: governance of witness infrastructure at national scale is unsettled, and no deployment exists at the scale of a national population of natural persons.

changeSets.title: Specify trust governance and cross-jurisdiction trust frameworks

anchorNote: p.35-36 l.392-427 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees
summary: Principle IX requires that compromise of any single component is contained rather than able to cascade (lines 407-408),…
text: Principle IX requires that compromise of any single component is contained rather than able to cascade (lines 407-408), and directs the health sector to build on national trust infrastructure where it exists (lines 415-418). Neither the principle nor any other part of the document says what that infrastructure must do about keys. Generation, custody, rotation, revocation, recovery and algorithm agility are unaddressed throughout, and there is no trust-anchor-failure model, so the containment requirement cannot be tested against any candidate service. The gap is substantive rather than editorial, and the vocabulary of the mechanism the guidance points at shows why. RFC 5280 section 5.3.1 enumerates ten revocation reason codes and distinguishes superseded (4) from keyCompromise (1), but none of them expresses recovery from compromise. The single reversible state is certificateHold (6), lifted by removeFromCRL (8), which RFC 5280 scopes to a certificate that 'expired or was removed from hold' rather than to a keyCompromise revocation being undone. A practitioner or institution whose key is compromised and who then regains control can be represented only as permanently revoked. DigiNotar remains the reference case for what an uncontained trust-anchor failure costs a country.
suggestion: State minimum key-lifecycle requirements and a trust-anchor-failure model, so that the containment requirement in Principle IX becomes testable rather than aspirational. Name the lifecycle states a national trust service must be able to represent, and include recovery from compromise among them and not revocation alone.

changeSets.title: Define a minimum security, privacy and audit baseline

anchorNote: p.57-62 l.373-414; also Figure 3.5 (p. 66) read as the printed page; section 3.4.5 agrees
summary: Section 3.4.5 makes an argument that the guidance does not then apply to itself. Terminology services, it observes, can…
text: Section 3.4.5 makes an argument that the guidance does not then apply to itself. Terminology services, it observes, cannot be relied on as runtime infrastructure unless the content they serve is governed, and the response is a full Semantic Governance Infrastructure with named roles, lifecycle and stewardship. The identical argument holds for trust: certificate and credential services cannot be relied on as runtime infrastructure unless the keys and credentials they serve are governed. Where semantics received a governance infrastructure, trust received an entry in Figure 3.5 and a referral out of the health sector. The asymmetry is a choice the draft makes rather than one it argues for, and a reader cannot tell from the text why semantic governance is health-specific while trust governance is inheritable.
suggestion: Apply the reasoning of 3.4.5 to trust. Either describe a trust-governance function at comparable depth, covering identity issuance and verification for institutions and systems, key and credential lifecycle, revocation and recovery, audit-log integrity, and the roles that steward them; or state explicitly why trust governance, unlike semantic governance, can safely be inherited from outside the health sector, so that the reader can weigh that judgement instead of inferring it.

sectionTitle: What REDDHI is and its foundational core
citation: §2.3 (Principle VIII) p.35 l.355-379; also Table 2.2 (p. 28) and Appendix C, Lifelong Health Record requirement 14 (p. 161)
anchorNote: Table 2.2 as cited
summary: Consent is well grounded in the principles: Table 2.2 names a health-sector consent service with consent enforced at th…
text: Consent is well grounded in the principles: Table 2.2 names a health-sector consent service with consent enforced at the point of data exchange; Principle VIII explains why the architecture does not set consent rules and anticipates a health-sector consent capability; the Lifelong Health Record is Required to integrate with consent management services (Appendix C, requirement 14). But the consent service named in Chapter 2 has no component specification. It is not among the twelve components of the Appendix C catalogue, so it has no functional requirements, no minimum data model and no conformance requirements, although every other load-bearing capability receives all three. The standards Chapter 2 points to, the IHE privacy and consent profiles and the HL7 FHIR Consent resource, are correspondingly absent from the component specifications.
suggestion: Give the consent service a component specification, or assign the capability explicitly to a named component and cite the applicable standards in Appendix C. Address withdrawal semantics directly, including what becomes of authorisations already granted when consent is withdrawn after data has crossed an institutional boundary, and state whether that case is in scope for DPI-H at all. EHDS Article 71 (Regulation (EU) 2025/327) is instructive here: it gives natural persons a right to opt out of secondary use at any time, applicable from 26 March 2029 under the phased timetable in Article 105, and Article 71(3) expressly preserves data permits and health data requests issued or approved before the opt-out was exercised. Even the most developed consent regulation on the books therefore stops at the institutional boundary, which is precisely why a component specification should say how consent rules are versioned, distributed and made auditable between organisations that share no common operator, so that the question of which rules governed a given exchange remains answerable afterwards.

changeSets.title: Specify consent and permissions as a first-class cross-cutting capability

anchorNote: p.77-78 l.926-951 read as the printed page; section 3.6.4 agrees
summary: Section 3.6.4 contains the document's strongest normative trust statement: a cross-jurisdiction trust framework, with m…
text: Section 3.6.4 contains the document's strongest normative trust statement: a cross-jurisdiction trust framework, with mutual recognition of identities, credentials and digital signatures underpinned by appropriate public-key infrastructure, shall establish that participants and the data they exchange can be trusted (lines 945-947). 'Appropriate' is undefined, and the GDHCN pattern cited immediately above verifies document provenance between national authorities; it does not authenticate live exchange participants, nor anything below authority level, such as a hospital verifying a foreign hospital or a clinician's role verified across a border.
suggestion: Specify what 'appropriate' must include: mutual recognition below the national-authority level via verifiable delegation from authority to institution to practitioner, key lifecycle and revocation, offline verifiability, algorithm agility, and no single point of control. Delegated verifiable identifiers extend the authority-level trust the GDHCN already establishes down to institutions and practitioners under the same framework, without creating a supranational authority.

text: Workforce licence verification is specified as a synchronous online query against a central registry, invoked at the point of care and therefore availability-critical (Health Workforce Registry requirements 8 and 22). The same guidance recommends offline operation for the Lifelong Health Record, HMIS and surveillance components, and Principle VII requires that the absence of continuous connectivity reduce what is available rather than lock users out. These requirements conflict in exactly the low-connectivity settings the guidance prioritises. Chapter 5 names verifiable digital credentials as an emerging technology (lines 8-9) but never connects them to the workforce credentialing APIs in section 4.3.4, their most direct application.
suggestion: Make the connection normative: a worker presents a cryptographically verifiable credential that verifies against cached trust state with no registry round-trip, with the registry acting as issuer and revocation anchor rather than as a synchronous verification dependency.

sectionTitle: Emerging technologies and the foundations they depend on
anchorNote: p.104-110 l.1-223 read as the printed page; section 5 agrees
summary: Chapter 5, Future proofing the Architecture, discusses AI, genomics, wearables and edge computing, but the document con…
text: Chapter 5, Future proofing the Architecture, discusses AI, genomics, wearables and edge computing, but the document contains no mention of post-quantum cryptography or cryptographic agility anywhere in its 254 pages. NIST finalised its first post-quantum standards in August 2024 (FIPS 203, 204 and 205), and lifelong health records are a prime harvest-now-decrypt-later target: data exchanged today must remain confidential for the lifetime of the patient. The term is also used loosely in the field. Programmes that describe a key-rotation mechanism as post-quantum readiness are describing something materially different from migration to the standardised post-quantum algorithms, and joint WHO and ITU guidance is well placed to hold that distinction for countries evaluating vendor claims.
suggestion: Add cryptographic agility as a design requirement for trust and exchange infrastructure: every participant must be able to migrate keys and algorithms without changing identifiers, breaking existing trust relationships, or coordinating a simultaneous global migration. Identifiers that commit to key digests rather than to a named algorithm allow the signing algorithm to change without re-establishing identity, which is what makes an unsynchronised national migration feasible at all. Ask countries to distinguish that architectural property from algorithm migration itself, and to require both.

text: WHO's Global Digital Health Certification Network appears twice: as an entry in the National Trust Services box of Figure 3.5, and in the cross-border discussion of section 3.6.4. Neither states the relationship a country should expect between its own DPI-H trust services and GDHCN participation, and the distinction that matters most is left implicit. The GDHCN pattern establishes provenance for documents exchanged between national authorities. It does not authenticate live exchange participants, and it does not reach below authority level, so it does not address how a hospital verifies a foreign hospital, or how a clinician's role is verified across a border. A reader planning national trust infrastructure could reasonably take the Figure 3.5 entry to mean that GDHCN participation covers cross-border trust in general.
suggestion: State in 3.6.4, and in 1.1.3 where the guidance discusses the foundations it builds on, what GDHCN participation does and does not provide, and how national DPI-H trust services are expected to relate to it.

anchorNote: p.11 l.102-113; also Figure 3.5 (p. 66) read as the printed page; section 1.1.3 agrees
summary: The section cites India's Aadhaar and CoWIN, alongside Estonia's X-Road, as evidence that health capabilities can be de…
text: The section cites India's Aadhaar and CoWIN, alongside Estonia's X-Road, as evidence that health capabilities can be delivered at population scale by building on foundational DPI. The examples are apt for identity and service delivery. Research whose corresponding author is at the WHO South-East Asia Regional Office has since added a second and more cautionary chapter to the same case, and the guidance would be stronger for carrying it. An assessment of FHIR implementation in India (Jain et al., Preprints.org, 24 June 2026, DOI 10.20944/preprints202606.1791.v1) records that although the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission is built on FHIR R4, it carries consent through a structured national construct, the MeitY Consent Artefact, 'instead of FHIR Consent' and rather than relying solely on SMART-on-FHIR patterns. The same paper records the omission of FHIR AuditEvent and Provenance resources and of OAuth2/OIDC scopes in patient-facing applications, and finds that ABDM certification 'primarily verifies connectivity (API availability, token flow) rather than data semantics'. This bears on the guidance directly, because OpenID and OAuth2 are the only identity-and-access standards Figure 3.5 names: the largest national programme built on that stack found it did not carry cross-institutional consent and engineered around it. The companion Sri Lanka baseline (Irfaan et al., DOI 10.20944/preprints202606.1768.v1) records that uncertainty over implementation of the Personal Data Protection Act 'creates hesitation among implementers regarding health data exchange, consent management, and legal liability'.
suggestion: Cite both assessments where the guidance discusses existing foundations, and let the India case carry its full lesson: foundational identity infrastructure transferred well into health, while cross-institutional consent required a construct built outside the standards stack the same programme had adopted. Three cautions belong with the citation. Both papers are posted as preprints and are explicitly marked not peer-reviewed. Their author teams are largely Indian and Sri Lankan institutions with a WHO South-East Asia Regional Office corresponding author, so they are regional research rather than WHO position papers. And the MeitY artefact is itself gateway-mediated and operator-anchored, so the case evidences how hard it is to carry consent across institutional boundaries rather than validating any particular remedy.

anchorNote: p.65-66 l.608-620; also pp. 80-81 lines 1036-1044 and Appendix C, Lifelong Health Record (p. 161) read as the printed page; section 3.5.2 agrees
summary: The guidance states that each component's requirements carry a status on a tiered model (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY) and that t…
text: The guidance states that each component's requirements carry a status on a tiered model (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY) and that the component descriptions are intended for use in planning, procurement and conformance (lines 609-610 and 618). It never defines what those keywords oblige. There is no reference to RFC 2119, RFC 8174 or any equivalent conformance-language convention; the string 'RFC' does not occur in the document, and 'normative' occurs once, in a note on ArchiMate modelling. Two further vocabularies then run alongside the first. Appendix C uses 'Required' and 'Recommended' (the Lifelong Health Record specification on page 161 alone carries nine instances of 'shall', six of 'Required' and one of 'Recommended'), and lines 1036-1044 introduce 'mandatory' and 'optional' as a support qualifier mapped to the IHE required/optional designation. That passage carefully reserves 'required' for one sense and 'mandatory' for another, which shows the drafters were alert to exactly this ambiguity in one place while leaving it open in two others. For the ministries, DPI authorities and procurement teams named as the intended audience, whether 'Required' in Appendix C is advisory or contractual once a country adopts the guidance is a first-order question.
suggestion: State the document's normative status explicitly in the front matter, and add a short conformance-language key that defines SHALL, SHOULD and MAY (RFC 2119 as updated by RFC 8174 is the usual reference) and reconciles all three vocabularies: the SHALL/SHOULD/MAY tiers, the Required/Recommended labels in Appendix C, and the mandatory/optional support qualifier. Say plainly whether the requirement tiers are advisory to countries, binding on implementations that claim conformance, or intended as procurement language that countries may adopt by reference.

text: The guidance already makes the important point that conformance to the same exchange standard does not guarantee semantic interoperability when implementations extend it differently, and it recommends nationally governed minimum data models. The mechanism behind that observation is worth stating: conformance to an extensible base standard does not by itself guarantee conformance to the same governed semantic model, so where implementations use divergent profiles or extensions, or where exchanged instances are not validated against a shared governed profile at the exchange boundary, two systems may both be conformant to the base standard while remaining semantically incompatible. This principle could be strengthened by requiring machine-checkable conformance to that governed minimum at exchange boundaries, including assurance that local extensions do not alter or contradict the shared semantics required for national interoperability. As one openly documented implementation example of this broader pattern, the Semantic Data Charter (Axius SDC) combines standards-based structural constraints, provenance and deterministic validation; it is cited here as an implementation example, not as a proposed dependency of DPI-H.
suggestion: Add a design principle to §3.6.2: "Local extensions may add context required by national or local use cases, but exchanged data should remain conformant to the nationally governed minimum model, and conformance should be machine-checkable at the exchange boundary so that local extensions do not alter or contradict the shared semantics required for interoperability."
reviewer: Timothy W. Cook; Luciana Cavalini, MD, PhD (co-author), Axius SDC, Inc., United States (Cook); Brazil (Cavalini)

text: As currently framed, the guidance prioritizes technical data transmission capability without explicitly linking exchange to clinical-economic workflow resolution. Data exchange is clinically and economically neutral without clinical transaction resolution. In both high- and low-resource settings, the highest leverage lies in managing treatment adherence and preventing chronic disease progression (e.g., managing hypertension and early-stage kidney disease to avoid stroke or end-stage renal disease). Line 102 
DPI has demonstrated impact in countries and catalysed ecosystem innovation across sectors.

Foundational DPI for identity, data exchange and digital payments — exemplified by India's Aadhaar digital identity, Brazil's Pix instant payments, and Estonia's X-Road data exchange layer — have shown tremendous value as shared infrastructure that can be leveraged by multiple sectors.

The health sector has been a direct beneficiary in some countries; for example, in India, the COVID-19 vaccination platform CoWIN was built on the existing Aadhaar identity infrastructure for beneficiary verification, helping deliver over one billion vaccine doses within nine months and reaching more than 940 million registered users. 

In Estonia, the  national health information system — which since 2008 has maintained a longitudinal electronic health record for every resident — runs on the same X-Road data exchange layer used across  all public services, while citizens access their records through the national digital identity (IDcard or Mobile-ID) rather than a health-specific credential . 

Together these cases show how  health-specific capabilities can be delivered at population scale by leveraging foundational DPI,  rather than building parallel identity, data-exchange or payment systems for health alone. 

The  health sector however, while not being unique in its ability to leverage foundational DPI,  possesses some unique requirements that have not yet been articulated to enable it to  effectively leverage these foundational components. 

This guidance articulates the explicit health-sector requirements that foundational DPIs would need to satisfy in order to contribute to health sector goals. Additionally, this reference architecture recognises that the health sector possesses some components that can be shared and reused across different programmes in  the health sector, components that can be described as health DPIs (DPI-H). 

It also articulates the explicit requirements that the “health DPIs” would need to satisfy in order to contribute to health sector goals.
reviewer: Filippa Pretty, Australian Collaborating Centre for WHO-FIC, Australia

text: The definition is useful and simple but remains health-agency and asset centred. A DPI should be judged not only by reuse across agency functions, but by whether it creates public value across a health ecosystem that includes people, communities, public and private providers, and subnational actors. text: We see the HMIS as having inherent properties of digital infrastructure, and thus this section has a major architectural omission: the two-layer model has no category for a shared public-health information and analytics platform. Foundational resources are restricted mainly to registries/LHR/terminology, while HMIS is placed downstream as a business application (data consumer). This misses infrastructure capabilities visible in mature DHIS2 deployments: an organisational hierarchy, metadata and indicator management, health workforce registries and user management, collection and triangulation of aggregate/event/Tracker data sets, analytics and GIS, data-quality and approval workflows, offline syncing, user notifications/messaging, and APIs. These core functions or registries may be derived, in some settings, from other registries (e.g. health facility registry), but in practice, these are often are built within and coalesce around the HMIS.
suggestion: Add a cross-cutting ‘Public Health Information and Analytics Platform’ capability, or recognise that a nationally shared HMIS/RHIS can itself provide infrastructural capabilities. Show that it can host reusable metadata, harmonise aggregate and event/person data, support multiple programmes, provide decentralised analytics and expose governed APIs.

summary: REDDHI makes registries and a Lifelong Health Record the common minimum, but excludes the national RHIS/HMIS platform t…
text: REDDHI makes registries and a Lifelong Health Record the common minimum, but excludes the national RHIS/HMIS platform that already constitutes the most mature digital health infrastructure in many LMICs. A DHIS2-based national RHIS often supplies shared organisational units, indicator metadata, aggregate data, surveillance, dashboards, APIs and a trained support ecosystem. Building new person-level foundations before strengthening this asset could delay value and fragment governance.
suggestion:
Define the REDDHI minimum through country priorities and installed capabilities. Add ‘shared RHIS/public-health information platform’ as an eligible core starting component in Table 2.2. Permit aggregate-first, surveillance-first and mixed-modality pathways, with registries/LHR added when priority use cases, lawful basis, coverage and operating capacity justify them.

Our point here is twofold. First, REDDHI "components" described in Tbl2.2 are all "foundational DPI"; yet registries alone cannot capture all essential facility-level aggregate, logistics, or surveillance data (many of which are cross-cutting!).  Second, business service layers already capture, combine, analyze, and extend those data along with the core registries. Thus, building on, learning from, or drawing on an installed base RHIS in the "business service layer" for development of foundational DPI, should be considred a key pathway for development towards REDDHI.
reviewer: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO), HISP Centre at University of Oslo, Norway

text: The local-capacity principle, because it focuses on design choises, is too narrow for platforms that become national infrastructure. DHIS2 sustainability depends not only on documented technology but on a distributed HISP ecosystem: permanent ministry teams, local HISP groups, universities, academies, implementers, help desks, peer networks and country-to-country learning. These relationships retain knowledge, support upgrades and turn local requirements into reusable platform improvements.
suggestion: Require a costed national capacity and support architecture: designated public-sector ownership; national and subnational core teams; local implementation/support organisations (HISP model as an example); university partnerships; academies, apprenticeship and mentoring; communities of practice; help-desk and escalation arrangements; succession; and recurrent budgets. Evaluate capacity as  infrastructure, to be developed and maintained over time--not as a one-off training deliverable.
reviewer: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO), HISP Centre at University of Oslo, Norway

anchorNote: p.34–35 l.346–379 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees
summary: The text states that consent is the primary mechanism by which individuals exercise control over their health data. Thi…
text: The text states that consent is the primary mechanism by which individuals exercise control over their health data. This conflates consent, legal basis, authorization and data rights. Public-health surveillance and many care operations may rely on statutory or public-interest bases; consent may not be freely given or operationally appropriate. Conversely, a lawful basis does not remove duties of transparency, minimization, security, correction and redress. WHO’s data principles similarly distinguish ethical data governance from blanket openness or consent: https://www.who.int/data/principles/
suggestion:
Distinguish: (1) lawful basis for processing; (2) authorization and role-based access; (3) consent where consent is appropriate; and (4) enforceable individual/community rights. Require purpose limitation, minimization, access logs, correction, appeal/redress, independent oversight and special safeguards for surveillance and vulnerable populations.

If limited by space, acknowledge that consent policies vary not only at the level of "systems that hold and exchange the data" but also within a system itself (e.g. public health surveillance may have different consent policies depending on type of disease or population). Consent resouces should contain at a minimum lawful basis, consent tupe, authorization and acces.
reviewer: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO), HISP Centre at University of Oslo, Norway

anchorNote: p.64 l.550–572; Box 3.1 read as the printed page; section 3.5 agrees
summary: The component criteria can be interpreted as a one-component/one-product procurement blueprint. This misrepresents plat…
text: The component criteria can be interpreted as a one-component/one-product procurement blueprint. This misrepresents platform architectures. A single DHIS2 deployment can co-realise aggregate HMIS, case/event surveillance, registries, facility profiles, campaigns, community information, analytics and feedback; conversely, one logical capability may be distributed across systems. suggestion: State prominently that components are logical capabilities, not mandatory software, procurement or deployment boundaries. anchorNote: p.89–92 l.63–197 read as the printed page; section 4.2 agrees
summary: Although described as adaptable, the phases remain infrastructure-first and largely waterfall. The DHIS2/HISP experienc…
text:
Although described as adaptable, the phases remain infrastructure-first and largely waterfall. The DHIS2/HISP experience demonstrates a different pathway: start from an immediate information-use problem; configure a minimum solution on a generic platform; implement in real work; learn through action research; and progressively generalise metadata, workflows and software. This is our experience how a platform grows from a useful local system into national infrastructure.

It could be argued that DPI-H evolution is different than RHIS, in that there is not a specific high-priority health data use case to target, but rather foundational functionalities with cross-cutting purposes. However, the "phased implementation" piecemeal approach could still be problem-oriented -- what have been the thorniest health problems to date, what would be quick wins, are there small foundational DPI-H investments that could show short-term results? This would reinforce the coalition of supporters over 2+ years to Phase 4, and also ties in with the "priority health goals" identified in 4.1
suggestion: Recast phases as iterative platform-building cycles: priority decision/use case → participatory configuration → minimum usable deployment → routine use and support → mixed-method evaluation → metadata/software adaptation → capacity transfer → scale or stop decision. In EP2 and EP3, explicitly allow existing platforms to be extended with new programmes and capabilities in each cycle.
reviewer: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO), HISP Centre at University of Oslo, Norway
