sectionTitle: The Role of the National Digital Architect
anchorNote: p.93–94 l.226–245 read as the printed page; section 4.2.4 agrees
summary: Assigning the architecture to ‘an individual or small team’ with a single authority risks a heroic-architect model, con…
text: Assigning the architecture to ‘an individual or small team’ with a single authority risks a heroic-architect model, concentration of power, bottlenecks to timelines, and turnover leading to loss of continuity. DPI-H decisions span public health, clinical care, law, privacy, enterprise architecture, implementation, gender/equity and subnational operations; no single professional can legitimately represent all of these.
suggestion: Specify a multidisciplinary, institutionally anchored architecture function with shared decision rights, documented accountability, subnational and user representation, conflict-of-interest safeguards, succession and knowledge management. sectionTitle: Design Data Structures and Data Models First
anchorNote: p.94 l.256–284 read as the printed page; section 4.3 agrees
summary: Calling data models the starting point, as a top-down approach, overlooks the public-health information cycle and how h…
text: Calling data models the starting point, as a top-down approach, overlooks the public-health information cycle and how health data is refined into health intelligence. In DHIS2, collection forms are not the analytical model (‘data input ≠ data output’); reusable data elements, dimensions, indicators, organisational units and workflows are configured from decision and reporting needs and evolve with use. A data model-first approach may simply digitise reporting forms and increase reporting burden. Evidence: https://docs.dhis2.org/en/implement/implementing-dhis2/conceptual-design-principles.html
suggestion:
Foundational facility and health workforce registries require minimal administrative datasets and may be the best place to start defining requirements.

Client registries: minimal dataset for capturing essential demographic details, both digital identifiers optional elements. Here we have found a logical model to be very useful, and a good place to start buildign logical models.

For terminology services, which will define the health data content of DPI-H, a longer and more thorough M&E review process is justified, going program by program and across administrative divisions. A level below that, EMRs will feed M&E systems and also inform clinical decisions; divergence of interests is greater across programs and regions.

To consolidate health program requirements, we recommend starting with priority decisions, users, workflows, existing reporting obligations and action pathways. Then define minimum reusable metadata—data elements, dimensions, organisational units, indicators, validation and workflow rules—separating collection interfaces from analytical outputs. Require participatory testing and iterative metadata governance rather than a one-off model-first exercise.
reviewer: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO), HISP Centre at University of Oslo, Norway

But, HMIS/RHIS is reduced to a ‘shared application component’ and explicitly declared non-foundational, even within business service layer. This underestimates the infrastructural role of a national DHIS2 platform: it provides shared organisational hierarchies, metadata, aggregate and event/person data, indicators, analytics/GIS, data quality and approval workflows, offline collection, notifications, APIs, extensions and a user/support ecosystem across programmes. text: The core attributes focus mainly at access, dashboards and dissemination. Platform features specifically desgined to support data use include user-specific dashboards, maps, interpretations/discussion, internal messages, alerts and action tracking. These features enrich decision-point convenings such as data review meetings, healthworker supervision and policy dialogues. In essence, HMIS should promote translation of data into information, and track actions taken by HMIS actors.  Evidence: https://docs.dhis2.org/en/implement/health/chis-community-health-information-system/implementation/data-quality-and-use.html
suggestion: Add ‘decentralised information-to-action and feedback’ as a core capability. Require role-appropriate analytics at facility, district and national levels; interpretation/discussion; configurable alerts; action plans with owners and deadlines; follow-up and closure; supervisory feedback to data producers; and measurement of whether information changed decisions or services.

anchorNote: p.218 l.4–24 read as the printed page; section C agrees
summary: The logical separation of PHSP (surveillance) and HMIS is defensible, but calling them distinct platforms is not. DHIS2…
text:
The logical separation of PHSP (surveillance) and HMIS is defensible, but calling them distinct platforms is not. DHIS2 supports indicator-based, event-based and case-based surveillance together with analytic dashboards, laboratory linkage, alert thresholds and emergency workflows. WHO-aligned DHIS2 surveillance toolkit deliberately triangulate case-based and weekly aggregate data. Such surveillance functions often overlap with and are sourced from HMIS; separate boundaries for HMIS and PHSP would duplicate metadata, users, hosting and support. Evidence: https://dhis2.org/disease-surveillance/

We see the primary distinction as one of governance, not business logic or functional requirements. For example, most countries have a designated agency responsible for infectious disease surveillance, within the MoH or an institute of public health. This institutional pattern is derived from two intertwined political mandates: to provide routine health services, and protect the public from epidemics. Often, the HMIS already captures monthly indicator-based surveillance datasets. So PHSP can use HMIS indicators as an early signal, in conjunction with its own case surveillance and contact tracing processes.

We further note that many countries also have developed ""public health emergency operations centres"", as evidenced during Covid19, when some countries special units were created under executive branches for on-demand health statistics and crisis management. Emergencies focused health leaders on identifying best-available data from all sources, leading to collapsed institutional constraints. This demonstrated an acute need for merged HMIS/PHSP models, linkages with lab systems, and collaborating with other ministries such as MET agencies and veterinary services.
suggestion: Describe HMIS and PHSP as distinct capability domains that may share a metadata-driven platform, organisational hierarchy, analytics and support ecosystem. Permit co-realisation in HMIS and PHSP where data segregation, privacy, access, performance and emergency requirements are satisfied. Acknowledge that HMIS and PHSP often share data sources, but serve different administrative structures.
reviewer: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO), HISP Centre at University of Oslo, Norway

text: The climate-related requirement is limited to ingesting sensor or data streams. Climate-informed public-health surveillance also requires compatible geospatial/temporal units, joint indicators, uncertainty handling, thresholds, cross-sector governance and explicit action protocols. Data integration without a decision pathway may produce dashboards without preparedness.
suggestion:
Expand the requirement to include governed climate–health indicator definitions, geospatial/temporal alignment, provenance and forecast uncertainty, alert thresholds, cross-sector data-sharing agreements, responsible decision owners, response protocols and evaluation of false positives/negatives and unequal impacts. In other words, these integrations have functional requirements as well as governance models. 

In more technical detail: we should also address the temporal and spatial resolution mismatch between climate data (often gridded, continuous, sub-daily) and routine health surveillance data (facility-based, weekly/monthly, point-located), since this reconciliation — not just data receipt — is the actual technical challenge climate-health integration efforts like DHIS2's Chap Modeling Platform have had to solve. Distinguish between passively receiving environmental data streams for monitoring/analysis and the more demanding case of climate-driven predictive/forecasting models (e.g., climate-sensitive disease forecasting), since the latter requires defining model outputs and decision-support integration as a distinct capability rather than framed around communicable disease surveillance.
reviewer: Brian O'Donnell (on behalf of HISP-UiO), HISP Centre at University of Oslo, Norway

text:
We fully support advocating for a recurrent line item in national health budget to signal government ownership of DPI-H. 

In addition to payment for recurrent domestic costs of running these systems, contributions to the technologies that underpin their DPI-H, particularly for digital public goods, would be strategic, cost-efficient, and risk free means for maintaining the technologies long-term. Contributions may take the form of DPG capacity building, feature suggestions, or in-kind support to the national innovation ecosystem around DPGs.

One direct contribution model, now underway through DHIS2 Shared Services Fee, offers a novel global funding strategy to sustain the digital public goods of DPI-H. If a country contributes even marginally to a pooled fund, then it directly contributes to a stake in  platform governance, security, and maintenance, which will have downstream benefits for their national DPI-H. We note tha without a durable funding stream for digital public goods, countries will either need to accept the long-term risk of product degradation, or turn to proprietary software vendors, which have been shown by evidence to be more costly on aggregate.
suggestion: Describe community contributions and pooled funding models as means to sustain DPI-H tools and capacity in the country.

text:
It may be useful to complement the CDSE's existing technical safety features and functional testing with a more explicit clinical-safety risk-governance methodology. The existing provisions around safe failure, continuity, governance, knowledge review and liability provide a useful foundation. A further layer of structured clinical-risk management could include elements such as a hazard log covering potential failure modes, a defined approach for assessing the severity of identified risks, and a clearly assigned role or accountability for overall clinical safety. 

These elements would align the framework more closely with established approaches to clinical software risk management, including the structures reflected in ISO 14971 and the UK's DCB0129/0160 standards. Including such a methodology as an explicit governance expectation could strengthen the overall clinical-safety framework.
suggestion: Suggested addition as an eighth governance consideration (p.189): '(8) Clinical risk management. Countries should maintain a structured clinical risk-management process for the CDSE, comprising: a hazard log recording identified failure modes and their potential clinical impact; a risk classification scheme for grading the likelihood and severity of harm; and a named, accountable clinical safety role responsible for the CDSE's overall risk posture. This should draw on established frameworks such as ISO 14971 and the UK's DCB0129/DCB0160 clinical risk management standards.'

text: Lines 315–321 appropriately distinguish the authoritative, technology-independent logical model from its FHIR representation. However, the subsequent recommendation to align underlying data models with FHIR resource structures may be interpreted as suggesting that the canonical semantic model should mirror the FHIR resource model. text:
The guidance assigns the national digital architect responsibility for architectural accountability, standards and conformance evaluation, while also recognising reviewers and assessors. It does not yet clearly distinguish responsibility for setting the normative baseline from responsibility for executing high-volume conformity assessment. In a mature national market, concentrating both functions in a small government team could create capacity bottlenecks and perceived conflicts of interest, and could limit the scalability of assurance.
The document's own "Public Governance" principle (1.4, lines 394–402) already establishes that components may be operated by public, private or non-governmental actors provided they remain accountable to public oversight - implying a distinction between the body that sets and safeguards the standard and the body that operates or is assessed against it. Section 4.2.4 does not carry this distinction through to the national digital architect role, which combines both functions.
suggestion:
Retain standards ownership, acceptance criteria and regulatory accountability with the national architecture or governance authority, while describing an assurance operating model in which testing may be performed by formally qualified independent laboratories, test centres or shared testing services against nationally governed test suites. Specify requirements for oversight, assessor competence, proficiency testing, quality assurance, transparent scope of authorisation, conflict-of-interest management and periodic requalification. Final conformity approval and regulatory accountability should remain with the competent national authority.

This is a distinct but related concern to the version-scoping proposed in comment 2: that comment addresses what a conformance statement should record, this one addresses who should be authorised to issue it.

This would extend the separation the document already establishes as a governance principle in 1.4 to the specific architectural role described in 4.2.4, rather than introducing a new requirement.

anchorNote: p.102–103 l.548–600 read as the printed page; section 4.6.1 agrees
summary: The financing chapter distinguishes how DPI-H is financed from what digital health financing can deliver. It could also…
text: The financing chapter distinguishes how DPI-H is financed from what digital health financing can deliver. It could also consider routine financing workflows as one possible implementation lever for interoperability. In settings where claims, reimbursement or provider payment are central to routine operations, standards-conformant digital submission may create a recurring operational incentive for adoption. However, an immediate payment gate could shift effort toward syntactic compliance, exclude smaller providers or create risks of service disruption.
suggestion:
Add an optional, context-dependent implementation pattern in which claims, reimbursement or analogous routine financing workflows are used as a phased incentive for standards-conformant submission rather than as an immediate binary gate. Couple this approach with semantic and data-quality validation, transparent rejection feedback, grace periods, exception handling, appeals or remediation pathways, and technical support for smaller providers. The guidance should note that the choice and timing of such incentives must be aligned with national financing arrangements, legal requirements and equity safeguards.

(For example, in Iran, hospitals are legally required to provide free inpatient care for accident-related injuries and subsequently submit claims to the Ministry of Health for reimbursement. Because nationwide compliance with electronic data submission was difficult to achieve immediately, the Ministry initially made reimbursement of these claims to inpatient hospital facilities contingent on submission of structured discharge data to the national electronic health record. In a second phase, basic public insurers similarly linked their hospital reimbursement to data submitted to the national EHR. This phased linkage between payment and EHR submission supported a transition to fully automated, EHR-based claims adjudication for inpatient services.)

(A comparable international precedent is the United States' Medicare and Medicaid EHR Incentive Programs-  commonly known as "Meaningful Use"-  under which providers received payment incentives, and later payment adjustments, tied to demonstrated use of certified EHR technology and structured data submission. The programme achieved rapid national uptake of certified systems, but was also found to shift provider effort toward meeting reportable data-capture criteria rather than toward the underlying clinical objective, and increased documentation burden on clinicians. This reinforces the need, noted above, for semantic and data-quality validation rather than syntactic submission alone, and for monitoring unintended effects on clinical workflow and coding behaviour when payment is linked to data submission.)

text: The data-quality and reconciliation requirement (line 126) and the availability and resilience requirement (lines 132–135) both note that the record must remain usable under intermittent connectivity, with reconciliation of duplicate or conflicting records and support for offline operation and synchronisation. The functional requirements table (row 19, 'Low-resource settings') similarly requires 'reliable synchronisation... when connectivity is restored'. None of these specifies how a conflict is to be resolved when the same record is edited concurrently at two disconnected points-  for example, two facilities updating the same encounter or medication list while both are offline. Given that the LHR explicitly supports federated and distributed deployment (row 18, 'Architecture flexibility'), concurrent offline edits are a routine rather than an edge-case scenario, and the resolution strategy chosen has direct clinical-safety implications.
suggestion: Add an explicit conflict-resolution requirement for offline and federated synchronisation, specifying at minimum: how concurrent edits to the same record element are detected; whether resolution is automated, and by what rule (e.g. last-write-wins, source-priority, additive merge), or requires clinician review; and how the audit log (row 20) captures the original, conflicting and reconciled versions so that the resolution itself remains traceable.

text: This is the correct position and the chapter does not address the strategic risk it creates. Broad semantic harmonisation across all domains is both the most expensive element of a national programme and the element most exposed to automation: normalising free text, mapping between code systems and reconstructing context from surrounding documentation are precisely the tasks language models are improving at. Countries reading this chapter may commit to the costliest and least robust part of the agenda.
suggestion: Distinguish what is robust under any AI trajectory from what is a bet on one. A small mandatory provenance set - source, method of measurement, time and status - is robust, because no model can reconstruct what was never recorded: whether a blood pressure was taken at home or in clinic, whether a diagnosis was a working hypothesis or a conclusion, whether a value was later revised. Broad semantic harmonisation is a bet. Recommend mandating the first, sequencing the second behind it, and setting an explicit review point. International estimates differ by more than an order of magnitude between countries that connect to existing standards and countries that model afresh, which makes this the largest single cost decision in a national programme.
reviewer: Hans ter Brake, HCI - Health Cloud Initiative, Netherlands

sectionTitle: Trustworthy AI in a health setting
anchorNote: p.108 l.155-168 read as the printed page; section 5.4.2 agrees

text: Section 5.4.2 states that before a capability is relied upon "it should be evaluated against representative cases and explicit criteria" and asks "how it was evaluated." This framing does not address the condition where the evaluation environment itself was compromised or misconfigured — producing evaluation results that appeared valid but did not reflect the system's actual behavior in deployment. In July 2026, two frontier AI laboratories disclosed that their safety evaluation environments had failed without detection, producing passing artifacts from compromised conditions. For AI components integrated into DPI-H, this creates a governance gap: a country may accept an AI system's evaluation results as evidence of trustworthiness when the evaluation environment did not accurately represent the health system deployment environment.
suggestion: After line 168, add: "Countries should require, as part of procurement and evaluation, that AI system providers attest that evaluation environments were isolated from production health systems and free from misconfiguration events during the evaluation period. Each AI system's disclosed evaluation results should identify whether findings are provider-attested only, or independently verified in a deployment-representative environment. This distinction is particularly important for AI systems deployed in clinical decision support and population health analytics roles."
reviewer: Dee Jared Johnson, Cognitive Fusion™, Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

text: Section 5.4.3 addresses equity and safety concerns in AI deployment, focusing on training data representativeness. It does not address a distinct equity dimension: the evaluation integrity gap is more consequential in LMIC settings precisely because independent verification capacity is most limited there. A health ministry in an LMIC deploying an AI-enabled DPI-H component based on a developer's evaluation documentation has fewer resources to conduct independent behavioral testing in its specific national health system environment. A country with limited AI oversight infrastructure has no mechanism to detect the gap between provider-attested evaluation results and actual system behavior in deployment.
suggestion: Add after line 176: "Countries with limited independent AI evaluation capacity face a compounded equity risk: they are less able to verify that AI systems perform as evaluated for their specific population and health system context. The guidance should advise ministries and DPI authorities in these settings to: (a) require AI system providers to disclose whether evaluation results are provider-attested or independently verified; (b) prioritize independent behavioral verification for highest-consequence AI-enabled DPI-H components; and (c) request evaluation environment integrity attestation as part of procurement — confirming that the evaluation environment represented the intended deployment context."

text:
The Ministry of Health of Slovenia welcomes this draft and considers it a substantial and useful piece of work. Our comments are offered from the position of a country that has operated a national clinical record since 2015 and is now extending it across several care settings through separately procured applications.

Our substantive comments concentrate on one structural matter, and we state that openly so the shape of this submission is clear. The guidance treats exchange, coded meaning and logical structure substantively, and each is given named standards or a named component. The persistence layer — the form in which a country's clinical data is held over a lifetime, and the standard that governs it — is not treated in the same way, and the places where the guidance does touch it are not consistent with one another. Because that layer determines what a country can do for decades afterwards, and because it is the layer our own experience bears on most directly, we have commented on each place where it arises. The remaining comments address conformance, cross-border flows, financing, workforce, the goal mappings, the country examples and a number of editorial matters.
suggestion: No change proposed. This comment is offered as context for those that follow.
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

citation: §General — register of inconsistencies in the treatment of the persistence and information-model layer p.Whole document l.see list
anchorNote: quotation found in the text

text:
This comment lists, in one place, every location the Ministry has identified where the guidance treats the persistence of clinical data or the information-model layer, so that the individual comments that follow are read as a set rather than separately. We have set them out this way because a reader encountering these passages in isolation will reasonably draw different conclusions from each, which is the opposite of what guidance of this kind is for.

WHERE THE GUIDANCE ALREADY ACCEPTS AN OPEN INFORMATION-MODEL FORMALISM FOR CLINICAL DATA
1. Annex D.1, page 230, lines 36–37 — EHRbase is listed under Lifelong Health Record as "an open-source, openEHR-conformant clinical data repository that stores and queries health data against openEHR archetypes and templates", alongside HAPI FHIR Server at page 229 lines 33–35.
2. Appendix C, page 175, functional requirement 2, status REQUIRED — the LIMR "shall support the representation of models conforming to recognised health data standards, including … openEHR archetypes and templates".
3. Appendix C, page 174, lines 81–85 — multi-formalism support is a core attribute; a national LIMR "should bridge between them rather than mandate one".
4. Appendix C, page 172, architecture placement box — the LIMR "is anchored in internationally recognised standards including HL7 FHIR StructureDefinitions, openEHR archetypes, and WHO SMART Guidelines data dictionaries".
5. Appendix C, page 156, line 43 — ISO 18308:2011 is cited as characterising an EHR architecture.

WHERE THE GUIDANCE NAMES ONLY FHIR, OR PRESCRIBES IT FOR PERSISTENCE
6. Section 2.2.2, page 28, lines 148–151 — the Open Standards enabling condition names HL7 FHIR, ICD, LOINC and SNOMED CT. No information-model formalism.
7. Figure 2.2, page 30 — the full-STAC "S" grouping lists HL7 FHIR, ICD, SNOMED CT, LOINC, CQL. No information-model formalism.
8. Section 2.3, principle II, page 32, lines 233–234 — "The architecture points to FHIR-based approaches as the direction of travel."
9. Figure 3.2, page 48, Shared Data Layer — the Lifelong Health Record element is annotated "FHIR-based store". It is the only element in the figure carrying a storage technology.
10. Figure 3.5, page 66 — the same Shared Data Layer is repeated with the identical "FHIR-based store" annotation.
11. Figures 3.2 and 3.5 — the Logical Info Model Repo element lists its artefacts as "FHIR profiles · eObjects · IPS · datasets". openEHR archetypes and templates are absent, contrary to item 2 above.
12. Figures 3.2 and 3.5, Interoperability column — openEHR is listed under "Open standards — Exchange & content". It is an information-model formalism, not an exchange standard.
13. Section 3.6.2, page 74, lines 811–820 — the paragraph naming the standards the architecture references lists nine, across exchange, terminology, identifiers, imaging and content. None for structure, although lines 805–807 state that the LIMR governs structure.

WHERE THE INFORMATION-MODEL COMPONENT IS OMITTED OR DEFERRED
14. Section 2.2.1, page 28, capability table — the LIMR is asterisked as "an enabler that can be built up as maturity grows, rather than part of the minimum foundation".
15. Appendix C, page 172, architecture placement box — "Countries should approach the LIMR as a progressive enabler, not an immediate prerequisite."
16. Figure 3.4, page 51 — the Metadata Components group lists the four registries and the Terminology Service; the LIMR is absent.
17. Appendix E, Goal 1, page 236, lines 238–240 — the foundational component list omits the LIMR.

WHERE THE GUIDANCE ARGUES THE MINISTRY'S CASE ITSELF
18. Section 3.6.2, page 74, lines 822–830 — "Standards designed primarily for data in motion are highly extensible, and uncoordinated extension produces what are sometimes described as interoperable silos."
19. Section 4.3.3, page 96, lines 319–321 — "A FHIR profile is a representation of that logical model, not a replacement for it."
20. Appendix C, page 173, lines 35–42 — two systems can exchange in HL7 FHIR "and still fail to interoperate meaningfully".
21. Appendix C, page 157, lines 107–110 — the LHR core attribute requires "storage of health data in accordance with the logical information structures published through the LIMR".
22. Section 2.3, principle VIII, page 35, lines 381–389 — the architecture should deliver "clear separation between the data a country owns and the systems that process it", with no mechanism named.

Items 6 to 17 are inconsistent with items 1 to 5 and with items 18 to 22. The Ministry's recommendation is that items 6 to 13 be amended to name an open information-model formalism for persisted clinical data alongside HL7 FHIR, and that items 14 to 17 be amended so that a governed minimum information model is treated as foundational.

If only one change is made, it should be Comment No. 8 in this excel — design principle II — because that is the sentence procurement teams will cite.

citation: §General — recommended treatment of clinical data persistence p.Throughout l.2.2.2 (p28–29); 2.3 II (p32); 3.6.2 (p73–74); Figures 3.2 and 3.5 (p48, p66); Appendix C (p155–179); Annex D.1 (p229–230)
anchorNote: quotation found in the text
summary: This comment states the Ministry's substantive recommendation in one place, so that it is not distributed across the in…
text:
This comment states the Ministry's substantive recommendation in one place, so that it is not distributed across the individual comments that follow.

The guidance should name an open information-model formalism for the persistence of clinical data, and should recommend openEHR archetypes and templates for that role, with ISO 13606 as the ISO-ratified equivalent, in the same way that it recommends HL7 FHIR for services and transactions in section 4.3.3. HL7 FHIR should continue to be recommended for exchange, and is also appropriate for the persistence of demographic, administrative and encounter data. Slovenia applies exactly this division nationally.

The reasons are matters of design intent and lifecycle cost, not preference. FHIR is designed for data in motion, as section 3.6.2 line 813 states, and its major versions introduce breaking changes — appropriately, because both endpoints of an exchange can upgrade together. A national record that persists clinical data in that form must migrate its entire data estate on the exchange community's release schedule; data at rest cannot run on a cadence set by the needs of data in motion. A two-level model, in which a small stable reference model is separated from clinical content governed as archetypes and templates, allows clinical definitions to change without migrating stored data — which is the outcome the guidance asks for at page 173 lines 55–59, where domain experts update definitions "without depending on software vendors to make those changes", but for which it names no mechanism. Provenance, versioning and audit are carried structurally for every data element rather than added profile by profile, meeting the LHR core attribute at page 157 lines 119–121. And the guidance's own observation at page 96 lines 335–338, that conformance is hardest to retrofit where underlying data structures are not conformant, applies with most force to the record itself.

This is not a position peculiar to Slovenia. Catalonia, already present in Annex D.2, has adopted openEHR archetypes for the clinical information layer of its electronic clinical history platform, and a Delphi consensus commissioned by the Spanish Ministry of Health reached the same conclusion independently. Three European health systems of very different scale have converged on the same division of standards by role.

The Ministry is not asking for exclusivity, and does not propose that FHIR be excluded from persistence where a country has chosen it. We are asking that the persistence layer be given a named recommended framework, as the exchange layer already has, and that the recommendation reflect what the guidance already accepts in Annex D.1 and requires in Appendix C.
suggestion: Three specific changes, each proposed in detail in the comments that follow: (1) in section 2.2.2 and Figure 2.2, add an open information-model formalism — openEHR archetypes and templates, or ISO 13606 — to the Open Standards enabling condition and the full-STAC "S" grouping; (2) in section 2.3 principle II, express the direction of travel by layer rather than as a single family; (3) add a subsection to section 4.3, placed before 4.3.3 and parallel to it, for example "4.3.x Clinical content and persistence: the governed information model", since 4.3.1 already establishes that data structures are designed first. Then align Figures 3.2 and 3.5 and the Appendix C material to it.
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

citation: §General — treatment of the persistence layer across the guidance p.Throughout l.3.6 (p71–78); 2.3 (p31–35); Figure 3.2 (p48); Appendix C (p155–179)
anchorNote: placed on the section, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (medium): Document-wide observation on persistence; the concrete ask is a new subsection in §3.6 parallel to 3.6.2.
summary: Reading the guidance as a whole, the Ministry observes that three of the four layers of a health data architecture are …
text: Reading the guidance as a whole, the Ministry observes that three of the four layers of a health data architecture are treated substantively and one is not. Exchange is specified in detail with a named recommended framework. Coded meaning is specified with named classifications and terminologies. Logical structure is given a component, the LIMR, with named formalisms in Appendix C. Persistence — the form in which a country's clinical data is held over a lifetime — is addressed once in the body, at page 74 line 830, and only to state that the benefit of aligned models holds "regardless of the underlying exchange or persistence technology". Yet the guidance does make persistence commitments: the LHR core attribute at page 157 lines 107–110 requires storage in accordance with the structures published through the LIMR; a functional requirement at page 160 addresses data storage; Annex D.1 lists both a FHIR server and an openEHR clinical data repository as Lifelong Health Record implementations; and Figure 3.2 annotates the record as a "FHIR-based store". The commitments exist but are scattered and are not consistent with one another. In our experience persistence is the decision with the longest consequences, because clinical data outlives the applications and the exchange-standard versions that move it.
suggestion: Add a short subsection to section 3.6, parallel to 3.6.2, addressing the persistence layer explicitly: what a country is deciding when it chooses how clinical data is held, why that decision has a different time horizon from exchange, the relationship between the persisted form and the logical models published in the LIMR, and the open formalisms available. Then align Figure 3.2, Principle II and the Appendix C material to it.
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

citation: §2.3 Design Principles — II. Open Standards p.32 l.226–238
anchorNote: p.32 l.226–238 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees
summary: This principle states that countries should ground implementations in open standards that "reduce dependency on proprie…
text: This principle states that countries should ground implementations in open standards that "reduce dependency on proprietary technology", and then names a single direction: "The architecture points to FHIR-based approaches as the direction of travel" (lines 233–234). No information-model formalism is named anywhere in the principle, and information models appear at line 235 only as something to be distributed, not as something to be expressed in a standard. This is inconsistent with the guidance's own treatment elsewhere: Annex D.1 lists EHRbase, "an open-source, openEHR-conformant clinical data repository that stores and queries health data against openEHR archetypes and templates", as an illustrative Lifelong Health Record implementation (page 230, lines 36–37); Appendix C page 175, functional requirement 2, status Required, obliges the LIMR to support openEHR archetypes and templates; and page 174 lines 81–85 make multi-formalism support a core attribute. A design principle that names one family as the direction of travel, while the component specifications require another alongside it, will be read by procurement teams as settling a question the rest of the document leaves open.
suggestion: Amend lines 233–238 to express the direction of travel by layer rather than as a single family, for example: "The architecture points to open, openly governed standards as the direction of travel — HL7 FHIR for exchange services and transactions, an open information-model formalism such as openEHR archetypes and templates or ISO 13606 for the logical structure of persisted clinical data, and established classifications and terminologies for coded meaning — while accommodating countries at different stages of readiness …".
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

changeSets.title: Define what 'open technologies' and 'open content' mean

citation: §2.3 Design Principles — III. Interoperability p.32 l.240–263
anchorNote: p.32 l.240–263 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees
summary: The Ministry supports treating interoperability as a structural property rather than a later integration exercise. The …
text: The Ministry supports treating interoperability as a structural property rather than a later integration exercise. The principle as drafted, however, addresses only one of the two ways a health system achieves it. Its whole substance concerns the topology of exchange — centralised mediator versus distributed capability, federated access, connectivity assumptions. Interoperability achieved at the data layer, where contributing systems write to and read from a shared, governed record rather than exchanging between themselves, is not distinguished from application-to-application exchange at all. The phrase "common data models" appears once, at line 244, undefined and unconnected to the Logical Information Model Repository that section 3.6.2 identifies as governing structure. In Slovenia's experience the distinction is the most consequential one a country makes: where contributing systems conform to one governed record, the number of interfaces to be built, tested and maintained falls with each system added rather than rising, and much of the exchange burden the principle discusses does not arise.
suggestion: Add after line 244: "Interoperability is achieved in two ways, and countries should be explicit about which they are relying on for a given flow. Data-level integration, in which contributing systems write to and read from a shared record governed by a common information model, removes the need for exchange between those systems. Exchange-level integration, in which systems that hold their own data communicate through standardised services, remains necessary across organisational and national boundaries. The first reduces the number of interfaces a country must build and maintain; the second cannot be avoided entirely. The design question is which flows belong in which category."
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

sectionTitle: What REDDHI is and its foundational core
citation: §2.2.1 REDDHI foundational core / Appendix C – LIMR p.28; 172 l.Table 2.2 (p28); architecture placement box (p172)
anchorNote: Table 2.2 as cited
summary: The capability table on page 28 marks the Logical Information Model Repository with a note that it is "an enabler that …
text: The capability table on page 28 marks the Logical Information Model Repository with a note that it is "an enabler that can be built up as maturity grows, rather than part of the minimum foundation", and the architecture placement box on page 172 advises countries to approach the LIMR as "a progressive enabler, not an immediate prerequisite". Both are in tension with the guidance elsewhere: page 173 lines 43–50 state that the LIMR "establishes the shared structural agreement before systems are built, rather than attempting to reconcile differences after the fact"; page 95 lines 265–273 state that data models should be defined "before implementation begins" and that the LIMR "is the designated home for these national data models"; and page 96 lines 335–338 note that conformance is hardest to retrofit where underlying data structures are not conformant. A ministry reading only the REDDHI table and the placement box will sequence the record before the model, which is the sequence the guidance warns against.
suggestion: Distinguish the two things now conflated. Reword both passages so that a governed minimum information model — the mandatory data elements for the components a country is actually implementing — is part of the REDDHI foundational core, while a full repository platform, with authoring, federation, dependency tracking and impact analysis, remains a progressive capability. Suggested replacement for the page 28 note: "A governed minimum model is part of the foundation; the full repository platform and its tooling mature over time." Cross-reference 4.3.1 and 4.3.3 from both locations.
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

citation: §2.3 Design Principles — V. Modularity p.33 l.286–301
anchorNote: p.33 l.286–301 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees
summary: The Ministry regards this principle as correct and, as drafted, incomplete in the one respect that determines whether i…
text: The Ministry regards this principle as correct and, as drafted, incomplete in the one respect that determines whether it works. Modularity is defined entirely in terms of component boundaries and interfaces — components "loosely coupled — able to be developed, deployed, replaced, or upgraded independently". Nothing is said about the data those components operate on. In practice, applications that each hold their own clinical data structures are tightly coupled through their data however well their interfaces are specified: replacing one means migrating or re-mapping what it holds, and the independence the principle seeks is not available. Slovenia's national programme is direct evidence. Its clinical applications are procured as separate lots, delivered by different suppliers, and can be added, replaced or extended independently — but only because all of them persist clinical content against one nationally governed information model. The modularity is a property of the shared data layer beneath the applications, not of the application interfaces above it.
suggestion: Add after line 294: "Modularity at the application layer depends on a shared data layer beneath it. Where each component holds clinical data in structures of its own, components remain coupled through their data however well their interfaces are defined, and replacing one entails migrating what it holds. Countries should therefore establish the governed information model for shared clinical data before, or alongside, the components that will write to it, so that applications can be piloted, replaced and upgraded independently against a stable record. A modular ecosystem of applications above a single standards-based patient record is the arrangement this principle is intended to produce."
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

changeSets.title: Clarify the shared data layer's scope and data responsibilities

citation: §2.3 Design Principles — VIII. Data Ownership, Access, and Control p.35 l.381–389
anchorNote: p.35 l.381–389 read as the printed page; section 2.3 agrees
summary: Lines 381–389 state the problem precisely: a government "can hold formal ownership of a system while lacking the practi…
text: Lines 381–389 state the problem precisely: a government "can hold formal ownership of a system while lacking the practical ability to access its data, modify it, or move away from the supplier that runs it", and the architecture should place practical control with the public entity "through open standards, documented interfaces, data portability, and clear separation between the data a country owns and the systems that process it". The Ministry endorses this without reservation. The principle names no mechanism by which the separation is achieved. Documented interfaces and portability are necessary but operate after the fact: they describe how data is retrieved from a system that has already determined its structure. Separation is achieved when the structure of the data is defined and governed by the public authority independently of any system, so that a system can be replaced without the data being converted. That is what an open, vendor-neutral information model provides, and it is the concrete expression this principle currently lacks.
suggestion: Add after line 389: "Separation of this kind is achieved most directly where the structure of the data, and not only its interfaces, is defined and governed by the public authority independently of the systems that process it. Where a country's clinical data conforms to an openly specified information model that it governs, a supplier's system can be replaced without the data being converted; where structure is determined by the system, portability guarantees access to data whose meaning still depends on the system that produced it."
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

text: Section 3.2 states at lines 127–132 that "an element shown in a view represents a capability or a type of component and the role it plays, not an instruction to procure a particular system", and that the architecture "leaves the choice of implementation … to the country"; line 117 describes the model as offering "a common structure and vocabulary, not a prescription". In Figure 3.2, however, the Lifelong Health Record element in the Shared Data Layer is annotated "FHIR-based store". That is an implementation prescription for the persistence of the national clinical record, and it is the only element in the figure annotated with a storage technology. The identical annotation appears a second time in Figure 3.5 on page 66, which repeats the same Shared Data Layer, so the prescription is stated twice and both occurrences need the same correction. Figure 3.2 is the artefact most likely to be reproduced in national architecture documents, so an annotation of this kind propagates further than the surrounding text.

Our recommended replacement is "openEHR / FHIR — stored in conformance with the national logical information model", which names both options the guidance already accepts in Annex D.1; "governed longitudinal store" would also be acceptable if no standard is to be named in the figure. anchorNote: p.48; 66 read as the printed page, no line resolved; in the cited section
summary: Three points on the semantic and structural elements of Figure 3.2. All three apply equally to Figure 3.5 on page 66, w…
text: Three points on the semantic and structural elements of Figure 3.2. All three apply equally to Figure 3.5 on page 66, which repeats the same layer, and both figures require the same correction. First, the "Syntax – Structure / Logical Info Model Repo" element lists its structural artefacts as "FHIR profiles · eObjects · IPS · datasets". openEHR archetypes and templates do not appear, although Appendix C page 175, functional requirement 2, status Required, states that the LIMR "shall support the representation of models conforming to recognised health data standards, including … openEHR archetypes and templates", and page 174 lines 81–85 describe multi-formalism support as a core attribute. The figure therefore shows a single-formalism repository where the component specification requires a multi-formalism one. Second, in the Interoperability column, openEHR is listed under "Open standards — Exchange & content" alongside HL7 FHIR, IHE and IPS. openEHR is an information-model formalism rather than an exchange standard; classifying it as the latter is the layer confusion this guidance elsewhere works to dispel. Third, the Terminology Service and the Logical Info Model Repo are both marked "Knowledge artefact" while the five registries and the Health Record carry the REDDHI marker; the REDDHI capability table on page 28 lists the Terminology Service as delivering a foundational capability without qualification.

Move openEHR from "Exchange & content" to a new grouping in the Open Standards column — for example "Information models" — containing openEHR and ISO 13606, so the column distinguishes the layers as the text does. Mark the Terminology Service as a REDDHI component consistent with the page 28 table, and mark the Logical Info Model Repo consistently with whatever resolution is adopted for the related comment on the REDDHI capability table.

citation: §3.3 The reference architecture in practice — Figures 3.2 and 3.5 p.48; 66 l.Figure 3.2 (p48) and Figure 3.5 (p66) — Shared Data Layer
anchorNote: p.48; 66 read as the printed page, no line resolved; in the cited section
summary: A constructive suggestion on the structure of the Shared Data Layer. The layer currently resolves person, workforce, lo…
text: A constructive suggestion on the structure of the Shared Data Layer. The layer currently resolves person, workforce, location and product into separate registry elements, each with its own governance, but represents all clinical content in a single "Health Record" element. In national practice the clinical foundation is not homogeneous: structured clinical content, demographic and administrative data, clinical documents, and codes and value sets have different structures, different rates of change, different retention requirements and, in consequence, different appropriate standards. Slovenia's national architecture decomposes its data layer accordingly — structured clinical data governed by an open information model, demographic and administrative data in HL7 FHIR, clinical documents through IHE profiles, and codes and terminology maintained on a national terminology server — with a common service layer and standardised APIs above it. Representing this distinction in Figure 3.2 would remove the need for a single storage annotation on the Health Record element and would show countries a decision they must in any case make.
suggestion: Decompose the Health Record element in the Shared Data Layer into its constituent data types — structured clinical content (openEHR), demographic and administrative data (FHIR), and clinical documents (IHE) — shown as one governed record with three typed stores rather than three separate records, with the applicable standard noted against each and the Terminology Service supplying codes across all of them. Alternatively, retain the single element and add a sub-line reading "comprising structured clinical content, demographic and administrative data, and documents, each governed by the standard appropriate to it" and add a list of standards so that it is not just FHIR: openEHR, IHE.
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

text: Lines 380–382 identify concepts deprecated without notice, version conflicts between systems, and national implementation guides drifting from the models they were derived from. Slovenia has addressed the third of these by requiring that every data-quality rule enforced in an application's user interface is replicated as an executable rule on a national validation server, so that conformance is established against the national model rather than against whichever application submitted the data. We suggest the Semantic Governance Infrastructure explicitly include executable validation of submitted data against published models, since drift is otherwise detected only when analysis fails.

summary: The Ministry endorses this section. The distinction drawn at lines 793–809 between governed structure and governed mean…
text: The Ministry endorses this section. The distinction drawn at lines 793–809 between governed structure and governed meaning, and the analysis at lines 822–827 of how uncoordinated extension of an exchange standard produces "interoperable silos", match Slovenia's national experience closely. The observation at lines 828–830 that aligning information models at the outset improves interoperability regardless of the underlying exchange or persistence technology is, in our view, the most important sentence in the chapter. citation: §3.6.2 Data and health content standards p.74 l.811–830
anchorNote: p.74 l.811–830 read as the printed page; section 3.6.2 agrees
summary: This paragraph lists the standards the architecture references — HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT and SNOMED GPS, ICD-11, LOINC, GS1…
text:
This paragraph lists the standards the architecture references — HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT and SNOMED GPS, ICD-11, LOINC, GS1 and IDMP identifiers, DICOM, IHE profiles and the international patient summary. Nine standards are named across exchange, terminology, product identification, imaging and content; none is named for the structure of persisted clinical data, although lines 805–807 state that the Logical Information Model Repository governs structure and lines 808–809 that both structure and meaning are required. Line 813 scopes HL7 FHIR to "the exchange-oriented representation of health data", which is correct and which leaves the structure layer stated as a requirement with no candidate named. A reader will reasonably conclude that FHIR answers both layers, which section 4.3.3 lines 319–321 states it does not.

Lines 828–830 note the benefit holds regardless of the underlying exchange or persistence technology. We agree, and suggest the guidance goes one step further, since countries must in practice choose. On the basis of a decade of national operation the Ministry would distinguish three roles: the logical structure of persisted clinical data, governed by an open information-model framework; persisted demographic, administrative and encounter data, for which HL7 FHIR is well suited and is how Slovenia uses it; and interoperability, APIs, services and transactions, for which section 4.3.3 already recommends HL7 FHIR. Making the roles explicit helps countries avoid adopting an exchange-oriented representation as a lifelong persistence format, where breaking changes between major versions of the exchange standard become migrations of the entire national data estate.
suggestion:
Two changes. First, amend the standards list from line 813 to name open information-model formalisms alongside the others, e.g.: "— among them HL7 FHIR for the exchange-oriented representation of health data; openEHR archetypes and templates, or ISO 13606, for the logical structure of persisted clinical data, within the EHR architecture requirements of ISO 18308:2011; SNOMED CT (and SNOMED GPS), ICD-11 and LOINC for clinical terminology and classification; …". Naming candidates at this layer, as the guidance already does at every other layer, does not mandate any one of them.

Second, add after line 830: "It is useful to distinguish the roles a standard is asked to play. The logical structure of persisted clinical data, the representation of demographic and administrative data, and the exchange of both between systems are different problems with different rates of change. Countries should select standards per role rather than adopting a single representation for all three, and record that selection in the information model and terminology components."
reviewer: Katarina Kralj, Ministry of Health, Slovenia

text: In answer to the consultation question on applicability across income settings, the Ministry offers the following about the limits of its own experience. Slovenia's ability to mandate a single national information model rests on conditions not universally available: statutory authority to require participation by all providers including private ones, a single payer, a national identity infrastructure already in place, and a population small enough for one editorial authority to govern one model. Countries without these will need different governance instruments to reach the same outcome, and the guidance should not imply that mandate is the only route. We would note, however, that the underlying recommendation is not weaker in constrained settings but stronger: a ministry with a small architecture team gains more from adapting an internationally curated, openly published model library than from authoring national specifications from first principles, which is the capability described at page 174 lines 104–108.

citation: §Annex D.2 – Country implementation examples p.233 l.151
anchorNote: p.233 l.151 read as the printed page; section D.2 agrees
summary: Annex D.2 does not include Slovenia. Slovenia is a relevant case for the Lifelong Health Record, the Logical Informatio…
text: Annex D.2 does not include Slovenia. Slovenia is a relevant case for the Lifelong Health Record, the Logical Information Model Repository and the Open Technologies enabling condition: a national record in production since 2015 in which persisted clinical content has been governed by an open information model throughout, while demographic and administrative data use HL7 FHIR, and in which separately procured applications from several suppliers write into one shared model. No entry currently in the annex illustrates that division of standards by role, or demonstrates supplier interchangeability against a single national model.
suggestion:
Insert after line 151, before the Spain heading (alphabetical order):

Slovenia
Components illustrated: LHR, Terminology Service, LIMR

Slovenia's national Central Patient Data Registry (CRPP), governed by the National Institute of Public Health, has held structured clinical data for the national population since 2015, with participation mandatory for all providers, public and private. It now holds over 330 million documents and receives approximately 200,000 new clinical records each day. Clinical content has been persisted against a nationally governed openEHR information model since the registry opened; demographic and administrative data use HL7 FHIR and documents use IHE profiles, with national code sets maintained on a national terminology server. Health workers can use their own information system or a nationally available professional portal (zVEM+) and citizens a portal and mobile application (zVEM) with some 560,000 active users (citizens), both served from the same governed record. There are several national digital services already built like ePrescriptions, eVaccinations, eReferrals and a recent national programme has extended this model with several national applications that run on the national patient record and platform: family medicine, paediatrics, community nursing, gynaecology, diabetes care, patient-reported outcomes and clinical documents, procured as separate lots and delivered by several suppliers against one shared model. It demonstrates how governing persisted clinical structure separately from the exchange format allows a national record to outlast the applications built on it, and lets capabilities be added without renegotiating structure each time.

Suggested footnote source: https://nijz.si/informatika-v-zdravstvu/ezdravje/ (National Institute of Public Health, eZdravje).

text: OMISSION — there is no guidance anywhere in the framework on the capture, transmission or storage of clinical photographs. IPC recently inventoried the use of digital tools by dermatologists worldwide across all regions (manuscript in preparation); dermatologists use a wide variety of digital tools, in particular for sharing psoriasis images. Images require quality control, consent, privacy, retention, encryption and interoperability, and a reimbursement system in every country. Given siloed healthcare organisation past and present, these images must be retrievable by other HCPs caring for the patient. Psoriasis is a systemic disease with comorbidities including cardiometabolic disease, depression and psoriatic arthritis, so care requires an infrastructure permitting interoperability and easy access for all healthcare workers involved. This matters especially in low-resource countries, where affordable, scalable, interoperable solutions can improve access to specialist care.
suggestion: Add explicit WHO guidance on consent, quality standards, retention, encryption and interoperability of clinical images as part of the Lifelong Health Record concept, together with the legislative/privacy framework and a reimbursement expectation. Guidance on privacy alongside the medical need for interoperability is mandatory.

Overall impression: I am so pleased to see the multi-stated and emphasised need for a true semantic data model as part of the interoperability framework, while also recognising no such thing exists yet, although open standard syntactic models and vocab models do which are great starting points to build on.
BUT, and it's a big but. When I looked for the patient-centred views of the system architecture i found very little evidence, except references to consent management and access rights control, all of which use language that assume a centrally managed method.  These are peripheral to an incredibly powerful perspective that this organisation centred view completely ignores. This model assumes an organisation first model for information management. While the data models defined and infrastructure models outlined could be utilised in a patient EMPOWERING way, the underlying theme is of a traditional org first IT style information management model. Patient empowerment in their information management is incredibly powerful as a means to deploy the infrastructure and data models you outline. Yet for a DPI for health, you miss any form of decentralised control model for information sharing, which can and should be an 'and also' mechanism for information flows, especially in countries either with highly decentralised health systems, or those, very common, legacy, highly fragmented care systems at the delivery edge made up of charities, private sector and publicly funded services.  The integration and governance burdens for small agile care providers are crushed by this reference architecture you have defined.  You have outlined many of the architecture components, it would not take much to give a nod to the need for decentralised models as an integral to this monolithic style organisational first model you have defined.
reviewer: Geoff Revill, Safe Space One Ltd, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

summary: DPI-H components (right set): Overall, I believe the proposed components represent a strong and well-considered foundat…
text:
DPI-H components (right set): Overall, I believe the proposed components represent a strong and well-considered foundation for national digital health infrastructure. The core registries, lifelong health record, terminology service and logical information model repository address many of the challenges countries face around fragmented data, inconsistent identification and limited interoperability. I also appreciate that operational systems such as EHRs, claims platforms and supply-chain applications are kept outside the DPI-H boundary while still being able to use the shared infrastructure.

There are, however, a few areas that could be clearer. Countries also need an authoritative way to identify healthcare organisations, not only individual workers and physical facilities, including provider groups, payers, laboratories, regulators and other participating institutions. Consent, authorisation, trust, provenance and service-discovery capabilities also need more explicit treatment, particularly where foundational national DPI cannot meet the additional privacy and consent requirements of healthcare.

I would also clarify the boundaries of some business-service components. For example, computable clinical knowledge can be governed nationally as a shared asset, while the engine applying that knowledge may operate within local clinical systems. Similarly, HMIS and surveillance capabilities may be delivered through centralised, federated or hybrid arrangements rather than through one national product.

Therefore, I see the proposed set as directionally right and a very strong baseline, but not necessarily a fixed or complete list for every country. It would be helpful to classify the components as foundational, context-dependent and advanced, allowing countries to sequence them according to their health priorities, existing infrastructure and level of digital maturity.
reviewer: Dr. Padmavathi Roy, United States of America

anchorNote: about the whole document, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (high): Online-form context assumptions (federated systems such as India).
summary: Context assumptions: In large, federated and mixed public–private health systems such as India, the guidance sometimes …
text:
Context assumptions: In large, federated and mixed public–private health systems such as India, the guidance sometimes assumes a level of national coordination and institutional authority that may not always exist. Responsibilities are often distributed across national, state and local governments, regulators, private providers and programme agencies. A single national body may therefore find it difficult to designate authoritative registries, enforce common standards or coordinate procurement across the entire ecosystem.

The guidance also assumes reasonably mature foundational DPI, legal clarity for health-data sharing, reliable connectivity and digitised source data. In practice, many settings still depend heavily on paper records, have multiple identifiers, experience unreliable connectivity and must provide care to people without formal digital identity. Consent and privacy frameworks may also be evolving or may not yet support granular, cross-organisational exchange.

Another assumption is the availability of specialist and financial capacity. Establishing a national digital architect function, FHIR profiles, terminology services, semantic governance and conformance testing requires skills and sustained funding that many countries do not currently have. Some remain dependent on vendors or short-term donor-funded programmes, making long-term national ownership difficult.

The guidance would therefore benefit from additional pathways for federated governance, offline-first implementation, interim solutions where foundational DPI is incomplete, regional sharing of specialist services, and a clearly defined minimum viable starting point for countries with limited capacity.
reviewer: Dr. Padmavathi Roy, United States of America

text:
Strengths: To me, the greatest strength of the draft is that it treats digital health as national health-system infrastructure rather than as a collection of separate technology projects. Its goals-first approach connects the seven priority health goals to the capabilities, shared components and standards needed to achieve them. This traceability helps countries make investment and procurement decisions based on health outcomes rather than on whichever product or technology is currently available.

The distinction between foundational DPI and health-specific DPI is another major strength. The guidance encourages countries to reuse national identity, payment and data-exchange infrastructure where it exists, while recognising that healthcare requires additional capabilities such as clinical identity matching, granular consent, longitudinal records, semantic interoperability and provenance.

I also value its practical and adaptable nature. REDDHI provides a direction of travel rather than imposing a rigid compliance model, and the guidance recognises that countries begin from very different levels of maturity. Its advice to assess existing systems, integrate before replacing them and progressively move away from fragmented programme-specific solutions is realistic and valuable.

Finally, the draft brings architecture, governance, interoperability, equity, financing and AI readiness into one coherent framework. Treating interoperability as a cross-cutting capability, emphasising governed terminology and information models, and connecting FHIR and IHE standards with conformance testing are particularly strong. Its message that trustworthy AI depends on trusted, representative and well-governed data foundations is both timely and essential. Overall, the draft provides a strong basis for a globally aligned yet locally adaptable reference architecture that can support progress towards SDG 3 and, over time, secure interoperability across organisations and countries.
reviewer: Dr. Padmavathi Roy, United States of America

anchorNote: about the whole document, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (high): Online-form concerns about operational detail across the document.
summary: Concerns / changes: My main concern is the gap between the strength of the conceptual architecture and the level of ope…
text:
Concerns / changes: My main concern is the gap between the strength of the conceptual architecture and the level of operational detail needed for countries to implement it. The draft explains the intended direction very well, but some essential implementation artefacts are still missing. In particular, Appendix E contains placeholders rather than the complete goal-to-capability-to-component mappings. These mappings should be included so that reviewers and countries can verify traceability, completeness and architectural gaps.

I would also like to see a clearer minimum viable architecture and maturity model. Countries need to understand which components are foundational, which are context-dependent and which are more advanced, together with measurable readiness criteria and decision points for progressing between stages. Additional implementation pathways are needed for federated systems, fragile or resource-constrained settings, incomplete foundational DPI, unreliable connectivity and significant dependence on paper records or donor-funded systems.

Some component boundaries also need clarification. The architecture should explicitly address a health-organisation and ecosystem-participant registry, as facilities, individual professionals and the legal organisations operating them are different entities. Consent, authorisation, trust, provenance and service-discovery capabilities also need clearer representation, particularly where foundational DPI does not provide the granularity required for healthcare. The distinction between nationally governed computable clinical knowledge and locally executed decision-support engines should also be strengthened.

The conformance section is conceptually strong, but countries will need reusable implementation profiles, test cases, reference datasets, certification governance and continuous testing requirements covering security, privacy, performance and version changes. A system implementing an accepted standard should not be assumed to “arrive tested.”

Finally, the financing section would benefit from a practical investment-case template covering total cost of ownership, recurrent expenditure, measurable benefits, risk, cost-sharing and transition from donor to domestic financing. Country examples should also use a consistent, evidence-based format that distinguishes pilots from population-scale implementation and records both achievements and limitations.

These changes would preserve the draft’s strong global vision while making it more actionable, measurable and realistic across different national contexts.

summary: Country / regional examples: Overall, the country and regional examples are valuable, but I do not think all of them ar…
text:
Country / regional examples: Overall, the country and regional examples are valuable, but I do not think all of them are sufficiently precise or evidenced in their present form. The draft sometimes describes a national strategy, partial rollout or collection of separate systems as though it were already a fully integrated, nationwide capability. Each example should clearly state its implementation status, coverage and date of verification.

The most important issues I identified are:

1. England:This example appears materially overstated. England centrally governs SNOMED CT UK and the dictionary of medicines and devices (dm+d), but this is not the same as centrally providing pharmaceutical decision support, including interaction checking, allergy alerts and dosage guidance, across primary and hospital care. NHS England explicitly states that dm+d does not provide decision-support functionality. It supplies terminology and information that other systems may use. NHS guidance also indicates that clinical-system configurations can differ locally. The example should therefore distinguish national terminology governance from decision-support functions implemented by vendors and individual care organisations.

 [NHS England: dm+d](https://digital.nhs.uk/services/terminology-and-classifications/dm-d)

2. India: The description of ABDM as a federated, consent-based architecture anchored on ABHA is accurate. However, the text should not imply universal implementation. The National Health Authority confirms that participation by citizens, healthcare facilities and private providers is voluntary. Likewise, official IDSP figures for 2025–26 show reporting rates of approximately 78–83%, depending on the surveillance form, not complete reporting by every unit. India should therefore be presented as a national architecture with substantial but still uneven adoption, especially across private providers and states. 

[ABDM FAQ](https://abdm.gov.in/FAQ) and [NCDC/IDSP implementation figures](https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/includes/About/CentresAndDivision/IDSP.php)

3. Kenya: The national HIE direction is correct, but its rollout status should be stated. An official Ministry of Health update reported that the Comprehensive Integrated Health Information System was operational in 17 counties in 2025, with expansion continuing. “A national HIE under phased implementation” would be more accurate than language suggesting complete national consolidation. 

[Kenya Ministry of Health](https://www.health.go.ke/government-scales-digital-health-reform-drive-accountability-and-efficiency)

4. Rwanda: The HMIS is a strong example, but the claims combine several capabilities that should be evidenced separately. WHO reported completeness and timeliness above 90% for public facilities in 2019, while only about 70% of private facilities were then reporting. The statement should not present the high rate as applying uniformly to the entire health sector. The claims concerning an OpenHIE-aligned longitudinal record, national decision support, laboratory integration and performance-based financing also need specific, current references. Rwanda’s newer National Health Intelligence Center demonstrates integration of multiple data streams, but this is not automatically equivalent to a complete national longitudinal-record exchange. 


The Spain, Catalonia and Tanzania examples are directionally accurate but need qualification. Spain’s HCDSNS exchanges selected clinical documents rather than providing a complete national health record. Catalonia’s HC3 and climate-health surveillance are valid examples, but access to social-care information should not be described as complete integration without current coverage evidence. Tanzania operates a national DHIS2-based HMIS, but describing it as “one of the more mature” systems is subjective and should be supported by current figures on coverage, completeness and timeliness.
reviewer: Dr. Padmavathi Roy, United States of America

Context assumptions: Gap 1: No regional interpretation layer.

Countries are left to independently interpret the WHO–ITU DPI-H Reference Architecture with no shared regional profile, resulting in duplicated interpretation effort and divergent architectural choices across otherwise similar health systems.

Gap 2: The WPRO RAF domains, while significant, still lack a technical execution arm.

The WPRO Regional Action Framework's socio-technical infrastructure and digital health solutions domains describe *what* countries should achieve but not the shared technical mechanism for *how* — a role AP-COIL's member labs, tooling, and testing mandate is designed to fill.

Gap 3: Countries will start creating reference implementations, but without coordination, these will not be interoperable with each other.

Unless organized through a transparent, regional networking approach, country-level work (such as the proposed Philippines' reference implementation on Open Health Stack – see Annex) risks remaining a single-country artifact instead of a reusable regional pattern other countries can adapt.

Gap 4: No feedback loop upward/region-ward. 

Country and regional implementation lessons rarely reach WHO/ITU or the emerging global open-source foundations (e.g., Open Health Stack Software Foundation) in a structured way.
reviewer: Alvin Valeriano de Borja Marcelo, Asia eHealth Information Network Community of Interoperability Labs, Philippines

text:
Strengths: Thank you for publishing a landmark document on a global digital health architecture built on digital public infrastructure (DPI-H). The Asia eHealth Information Network (AeHIN), created by the World Health Organization in 2012, has long espoused the Mind/Fill the GAPS framework, in which “Architecture” is a key component. Our comments and suggestions are as follows:

Observation 1. The WHO–ITU Reference Architecture Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for Health (DPI-H) gives countries advice on the TOGAF/ArchiMate-based enterprise architecture framework — organized around seven priority health goals and the REDDHI (Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health Infrastructure) concept — for moving from strategic intent to coherent technical implementation. It is explicitly designed as a technology-neutral blueprint that individual countries adapt to their own context, not a single deployable system. The work is comprehensive and solid.

Observation 2. A regional framework already exists to receive it. The Regional Action Framework on Digital Health in the Western Pacific, endorsed by Member States at the 75th WHO Regional Committee for the Western Pacific (2024), organizes country actions around five domains — governance, socio-technical infrastructure, financing and economics, digital health solutions, and data — guided by principles of equity, open innovation, accountability, pragmatism, and sustainability. Member-state consultations during its formulation repeatedly surfaced standards and interoperability (the S in GAPS) and governance and leadership (the G in GAPS) as the priorities countries most need help operationalizing.
reviewer: Alvin Valeriano de Borja Marcelo, Asia eHealth Information Network Community of Interoperability Labs, Philippines
