Concerns / changes: Summary Action: Build a community of practice around the Reference Architecture

To fill these translation gaps, the Asia eHealth Information Network, together with the Pacific Health Information Network, jointly announce the creation of the Asia-Pacific COIL (AP-COIL).

The goals of AP-COIL are:

1. Rapid, systematic, structured dissemination of the WHO-ITU Reference Architecture. AeHIN and PHIN will host webinars and feature resource persons from WHO-ITU as speakers. The regional networks will pull in the right audience in each region and country.

2. Formalizing the Asia-Pacific Community of Interoperability Labs (AP-COIL) as a community of practice aligning the global, regional, and national reference architectures. WPRO/SEARO regional experts will be invited to provide guidance and oversight.

3. Empowering the AP-COIL to craft the regional implementation guides along with a regional reference implementation on Open Health Stack (tbc). This regional effort can begin from the best practices and lessons learned from the International Patient Summary for the Hajj as a use case.

4. Committing the AP-COIL members to continuously connect their country's efforts to the regional interoperability blueprint and ensure alignment through continuous knowledge sharing.

Attached as Part 2 are the AP-COIL Concept Note (Part 2) and the proposal for a Philippine-specific reference implementation using OpenHealthStack (annex). Both are needed to show alignment of the WHO-ITU Reference Architecture for Digital Public Infrastructure with the WPRO/SEARO Regional Action Frameworks and a national digital health strategy.

text:
Concerns / changes: The guidance underserves the last-mile implementation context. Community health workers are the primary point of contact for the majority of people that DPI-H is intended to reach, yet the architecture is largely described from the perspective of facility-based systems and national platforms. Offline-first data synchronization, which is essential in low-connectivity field environments, receives minimal treatment. From direct experience managing data synchronization across 250,000 household records in rural field conditions, the failure modes that matter most that is partial sync conflicts, device-level data loss, bandwidth-constrained record capture  are not addressed in the current draft.

The guidance would be significantly stronger with a dedicated section on last-mile architecture considerations, covering offline-capable data collection, CHW-facing application requirements, and how community-level data flows connect to national registries. Tools like KoboToolbox, ODK, and CommCare are widely used across Sub-Saharan Africa for exactly this purpose but are not meaningfully referenced in the implementation guidance.

text:
DPI-H components (right set): Broadly, yes. The proposed components represent a coherent and useful core set for national digital health infrastructure, particularly the Client, Facility, Workforce and Product Registries, the Lifelong Health Record, Terminology Service, Logical Information Model Repository, Computable Decision Support Engine, HMIS and Public Health Surveillance Platform.

I particularly support the distinction between shared foundational components and reusable business-service components, rather than treating programme-specific applications as DPI-H.

My main reservation is not that major components are missing, but that several cross-cutting capabilities need more explicit architectural treatment. Consent and permissions management is described as a foundational REDDHI capability and is required by the Lifelong Health Record, but it is not articulated with the same level of interface and lifecycle detail as the named components. Similarly, learned AI/ML models may be deployed across several components or point-of-service systems, but the architecture would benefit from a cross-cutting lifecycle profile covering model identity, versioning, validation, monitoring and accountability.

I would therefore retain the proposed component set while strengthening these cross-cutting service profiles rather than necessarily adding new centralised components.

Context assumptions: The guidance is generally strong in recognising different levels of digital maturity, resource availability and connectivity, so I do not see a major assumption that all countries start from similar conditions.

However, implementation may still implicitly depend on institutional capacities that are uneven across settings: sustained governance of shared national components, clear assignment of data stewardship and decision rights, technical capacity to maintain standards and information models over time, and the ability to enforce consistent access and consent policies across fragmented or federated systems.

In lower-capacity settings, reliable connectivity, mature national identity infrastructure, specialist interoperability expertise and long-term financing may also be incomplete or unstable. I therefore suggest distinguishing more explicitly between capabilities that may mature progressively and minimum non-negotiable properties-particularly security, auditability, provenance and safe handling of conflicting data-that should remain required even at early stages of implementation.

Offline and federated environments deserve particular attention: "reliable synchronisation" is necessary, but clinically significant conflicting updates need explicit minimum conflict-resolution and reconciliation rules.

summary: Strengths: The greatest strength is that the guidance treats digital health infrastructure as shared national capabilit…
text:
Strengths: The greatest strength is that the guidance treats digital health infrastructure as shared national capability rather than as a collection of disease-specific or programme-specific systems. This directly addresses fragmentation, duplicated investment and vendor dependency.

A second major strength is the clear distinction between foundational DPI and health-specific DPI-H, allowing health systems to build on national identity, payment and data-exchange infrastructure without assuming that general-purpose DPI can meet all health-sector requirements.

Third, interoperability is treated correctly as a cross-cutting architectural property rather than as a single middleware product. The combination of open standards, semantic governance, terminology services, common information models and conformance testing gives the architecture substantially more implementation value than a high-level policy framework alone.

Finally, REDDHI is a useful concept because it provides countries with a direction of travel and a minimum foundation without presenting the architecture as a single fixed end-state. The emphasis on different starting points, progressive implementation and national adaptation makes the guidance relevant across different levels of digital maturity.

anchorNote: about the whole document, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (medium): Several cross-cutting concerns (consent, AI lifecycle, sync) spanning chapters.
summary: Concerns / changes: My main concerns are not with the overall architecture, but with several cross-cutting requirements…
text:
Concerns / changes: My main concerns are not with the overall architecture, but with several cross-cutting requirements that would benefit from more explicit and testable specification.

1. Consent and permissions architecture. Consent and authorisation are treated as foundational capabilities, and the Lifelong Health Record depends on consent-management services, but the architecture does not provide an equivalent cross-cutting service profile defining consent representation, lifecycle, interfaces, revocation propagation, delegated/proxy authority and audit.

2. AI/ML lifecycle governance. Chapter 5 provides strong principles for responsible AI, including evaluation, equity, human oversight and monitoring for drift. However, learned models used across decision support, analytics, surveillance or point-of-service applications should be traceable to a unique model/version, accountable owner, intended use, validation evidence, deployment status and monitoring state.

3. Longitudinal record lifecycle. The LHR appropriately emphasises immutable history and provenance, but the requirement that records should “never be deleted” should be reconciled more explicitly with correction of wrong-person attribution, logical withdrawal and legally required erasure.

4. Offline and federated consistency. The guidance supports offline operation and federated architectures, but minimum semantics for conflicting concurrent updates should be clearer. Clinically material conflicts should not be silently overwritten or presented as a single authoritative fact before reconciliation.

5. Minimum security floor. Graduated assurance is appropriate for countries with different levels of maturity, but essential security properties-authentication, authorisation, least privilege, confidentiality, auditability, integrity and recovery-should remain explicit minimum requirements even where more advanced assurance mechanisms are introduced progressively.

Addressing these issues would make the architecture more implementable and testable without making it more prescriptive about specific technologies.

text:
Concerns / changes: While Norway/IMDI strongly supports the overall direction of the guidance, several areas could be strengthened further.
We acknowledge WHOs important role in sharing knowledge, guiding and promoting alignment in health architecture globally. We understand that the primary audience for this guidance is at national-level focusing on national implementation. However, we do believe that the document would benefit from a stronger global perspective as health challenges inevitably transcend national boundaries, and consequently pandemics, public health surveillance, cross-border healthcare, international research collaboration, and global data sharing require cross border considerations. WHO's normative role and existing global public goods facilitates such collaboration, and we recommend this to be more explicitly leveraged throughout this guidance document. (Specified in bullet point 1).

Under this heading, Norway/IMDI recommends a stronger emphasis on WHO's own terminologies and classifications. WHO-FIC, including ICD, ICF, ICHI, and ATC, ICD-O and others, should be positioned as primary reference models whenever semantic interoperability and terminology governance are discussed. These internationally governed and widely adopted systems provide an important foundation for global comparability, data reuse, and equitable access. We therefore specifically recommend references to WHO standards to precede references to non-WHO terminologies, which may instead be presented as complementary solutions where appropriate. (Specified in bullet point 2). For some background, see: https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/clinician-documentation-hub).

We also suggest that you may consider highlighting use of WHO products in AI.  As mentioned above, the WHO-FIC Foundation provides a globally governed semantic resource that can support trusted AI applications through standardized concepts and classifications (https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/icd-11-implementation, see bullet point 28).

We further suggest that the guidance would benefit from greater visibility of WHO's mature governance models. The longstanding governance arrangements supporting WHO classifications demonstrate how Member States, clinicians, technical experts, and subject-matter specialists can collaborate to develop and maintain global health standards. Including these experiences in the consideration or as examples could provide valuable lessons for countries establishing their own governance structures (https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/who-fic-family-paper). (Specified in bullet point 3).

Finally, Norway/IMDI recommends strengthening the strategic role of clinical and public health leadership within the governance framework. While clinical expertise is referenced throughout the document, clinical governance does not appear to be given the same strategic prominence as architecture, security, and interoperability governance. Based on Norway/IMDI's experience, a key factor for succeeding on in digital health architecture development, is to involve clinical and public health expertise throughout all stages of development and implementation, including at the highest decision-making levels. This ensures patient safety, quality of care, and public health objectives are adequately addressed also under the development of digital architecture.
reviewer: Information Management and Methods Division, The Norwegian Directorate of Health, Norway

text:
DPI-H components (right set): Leverage IHE's Foundational Work as an Implementation Layer

IHE specifications complement standards such as HL7 FHIR, DICOM, HL7 CDA or HL7 v2, and could similarly complement the terminology standards referenced by the draft WHO handbook. IHE provides the use-case aggregation and definition, together with the implementation layer that makes those standards work together in real clinical and operational workflows. IHE profiles define actor responsibilities, coordinated transactions, content and terminology constraints, required options, cross-profile dependencies, and testable conformance expectations.

The draft already applies this approach in selected areas, notably its use of IHE Mobile Care Services Discovery (mCSD) for facility and workforce registry functions and IHE Sharing Valuesets, Codes, and Maps (SVCM) for terminology services. The same discipline should be applied consistently across the architecture. The following examples are illustrative rather than exhaustive and should be validated against the final DPI-H use cases and selected profile versions.

DPI-H capability

1. Client identity and matching
   Illustrative IHE assets: PIXm, PDQm, PMIR
   How the assets can be leveraged: Patient identity query, cross-referencing, synchronization, and merge patterns.

2. Facility, workforce, service and endpoint directories
   Illustrative IHE assets: mCSD
   How the assets can be leveraged: Federated discovery and update of organizations, practitioners, locations, services, and exchange endpoints.

3. Lifelong record and document exchange
   Illustrative IHE assets: MHD, MHDS, XDS.b
   How the assets can be leveraged: Mobile/FHIR-based and established document-sharing patterns that can support distributed or hybrid architectures.

4. Federated and cross-border discovery and access
   Illustrative IHE assets: XCA, XCPD
   How the assets can be leveraged: Gateway, patient discovery, query, and retrieval patterns across autonomous communities and jurisdictions.

5. Terminology services
   Illustrative IHE assets: SVCM
   How the assets can be leveraged: Standards-based sharing and use of code systems, value sets, and concept maps.

6. International Patient Summary exchange
   Illustrative IHE assets: sIPS
   How the assets can be leveraged: A workflow profile for sharing IPS content using established actors and transactions.

7. Trust, authorization, audit and consent
   Illustrative IHE assets: ATNA, IUA, BALP, XUA, PCF
   How the assets can be leveraged: Reusable security, authorization, audit-event, user-assertion, and consent patterns.

8. Diagnostic imaging exchange
   Illustrative IHE assets: XDS-I, XCA-I and IHE Radiology profiles
   How the assets can be leveraged: Standards-based discovery and exchange of imaging information across enterprises and communities.

Illustrative mapping only; profile selection should be governed by the final use case, applicable options, dependencies, version, and testing requirements.

Additional comment on Introduction and health goals (Sections 1.4–1.5, 2.4 and Appendix E)

Make each health goal traceable to a clinical or operational workflow, the international profiles that support it, and measurable acceptance criteria. Validate these links with clinicians, patients, public-health users, and implementers. Apply the global-core, national-extension principle to this mapping.
reviewer: Aaron Goldmuntz, IHE International, United States of America

changeSets.title: Adopt a global-core, national-extension policy for standards and profiles

anchorNote: placed on the section, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (medium): Concern about national profile/specification guidance; cites 3.6.2 and 4.3, chiefly 4.3.
summary: Context assumptions: Prevent National Implementation Guidance from Recreating Fragmentation
text:
Context assumptions: Prevent National Implementation Guidance from Recreating Fragmentation

The primary concern arises as the draft moves from the global reference architecture to national implementation. Sections 3.6.2 and 4.3 state that standards selection and binding are made nationally and that countries should define minimum data models, actors, roles, services, transactions, and FHIR-based profiles. National governance is indispensable, but these passages could be interpreted as inviting every country to create its own technical specifications for requirements that are fundamentally shared across borders.

That approach would risk producing different national interpretations of the same base standards, duplicative specification and testing costs, country-by-country customization for suppliers, reduced portability of solutions, and new barriers to regional and cross-border exchange. It would also impose the greatest burden on countries with the fewest standards-development and testing resources. In practical terms, it could propagate the 'interoperable silos' that the draft itself correctly warns against. This also impacts the ability for the industry to consistently implement the specifications across different jurisdictions and for the national authorities to provide coordinated test beds to validate such implementations (e.g. at IHE Connectathons, or through Projectathons).

National programs should retain authority over law, policy, governance, consent, language, terminology localization, implementation validation, procurement, and truly jurisdiction-specific workflows. They should not independently redefine reusable actors, transactions, APIs, security patterns, or information structures and terminologies when suitable international specifications already exist. Local requirements should be implemented as governed extensions to a common international core, with clear provenance, versioning, and conformance rules.
reviewer: Aaron Goldmuntz, IHE International, United States of America

Strengths: IHE International appreciates the opportunity to comment on this important draft. We strongly support its central premises: health digital public infrastructure should be built on shared foundations; interoperability should be treated as a cross-cutting capability rather than a single product or middleware layer; implementations should rely on open, publicly governed specifications; and conformance should be testable. These principles are closely aligned with IHE's mission and with more than 25 years of work profiling international standards into implementable, testable interoperability specifications.

We particularly welcome Sections 3.6 and 3.7, including the recognition in Section 3.7.3 that IHE is a principal example of a framework that can be accommodated directly within the reference architecture. The draft appropriately explains that, where an interaction corresponds to an IHE transaction, the architecture can defer to the IHE specification for protocol details and to IHE conformance tooling for testing. That is an important and accurate foundation.

anchorNote: about the whole document, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (medium): General 'global core, national extension' policy recommendation.
summary: Concerns / changes: IHE strongly endorses the overall direction of the guidance and its emphasis on shared foundations,…
text:
Concerns / changes: IHE strongly endorses the overall direction of the guidance and its emphasis on shared foundations, interoperability, and testable conformance. Our recommendations are intended to strengthen this foundation and support consistent, sustainable implementation. In particular, an explicit global-core, national-extension approach, supported by reuse of international profiles and testing resources, would help countries put the guidance into practice while reducing duplication.

Core recommendation: Adopt an explicit 'global core, national extension' policy. Countries should first reuse applicable international standards and IHE profiles. When a genuine gap exists, countries and regional bodies should work with the relevant international Standards Development Organizations and established profiling organizations through open, consensus-based processes. National specifications should be limited to transparent extensions or constraints needed for jurisdiction-specific policy and practice, while preserving interoperability with the international core.

Publish and maintain a living DPI-H-to-standards mapping

WHO and ITU should publish a maintained companion mapping from each DPI-H component, actor, service, and interaction to applicable international standards and profiles. For each entry, the mapping should identify the relevant actor or role, transaction or operation, status and version, dependencies, conformance resources, and known gaps. The current draft's detailed use of mCSD and SVCM provides a strong model, but similarly relevant IHE assets should be surfaced for e.g. identity, document exchange, federated access, trust, audit, consent, IPS exchange, and imaging.

Offer of Collaboration

IHE International is ready to collaborate with WHO, ITU, GDHP international SDOs - through the JIC, OpenHIE, countries, and the vendor and clinical communities to make this architecture actionable. IHE can support a detailed mapping of DPI-H components and interactions to existing IHE profiles; route identified gaps through its international domain committees and open public-comment process; advance new or updated specifications through trial implementation; contribute test plans, tools, and reference data; coordinate global and regional Connectathons and exploratory testing events; and help countries develop procurement language grounded in verifiable interoperability requirements.

This collaboration would reduce duplication, improve the consistency and maintainability of national implementations, strengthen supplier accountability, and accelerate regional and cross-border interoperability. It would also allow investments made in one country to contribute to a reusable global public good.

The essential message is simple: national adaptation should build on a shared international core, not create a new core for every country. IHE stands ready to help WHO and ITU translate that principle into profiles, testable requirements, and a robust global implementation ecosystem.

summary: Make international reuse a cross-cutting design principle
text:
Make international reuse a cross-cutting design principle

The 'global core, national extension' principle should appear in the Executive Summary, the DPI-H design principles, Section 3.6.2, and the opening of Section 4.3. Repetition is warranted because these sections reach different audiences. The guidance should make clear that open standards are not merely documents to cite; they are governed by international communities and lifecycle processes that country representatives are invited to and should engage in.

Add standards and profile discovery before national specification

Before a country designs a new model, actor, transaction, API, or test, the implementation method should require a documented landscape review. That review should map each DPI-H capability and interaction to applicable international standards, IHE profiles, other established implementation guides, and available test assets. Only residual, unmet requirements should enter a national gap analysis and ultimately an effort to standardize the solution across the ecosystem.

Route generalizable gaps into international consensus processes

When the architecture identifies a missing international specification, the default response should not be a separate national invention. WHO and ITU should encourage countries to submit the need, use case, and proposed requirements to the responsible international SDO or profiling organization. This is especially relevant where the draft itself identifies an active standardization gap, such as interaction models for Logical Information Model Repository capabilities. A shared backlog would enable expert review, implementation feedback, public comment, coordinated maintenance, and reuse by many countries.

The Global Digital Health Partnership (GDHP) as collaboration of national digital health agencies and WHO through its engagement with the Joint Initiative Council (JIC) of all relevant digital health standardization organizations provides a venue for this, as has been demonstrated with the International Patient Summary specifications.
suggestion:
Proposed cross-cutting principle

Countries should adopt a global-core, national-extension approach. Before creating a new data model, actor, transaction, interface, terminology definition or implementation profile, national programs should evaluate and reuse applicable specifications maintained by recognized international Standards Development Organizations and established profiling organizations. National requirements should be expressed as transparent extensions or constraints that preserve interoperability with the international core. When a generalizable gap is identified, countries and regional bodies should work with the responsible international organization through an open, consensus-based process so that the resulting specification can be reviewed, tested, maintained, and reused globally.

Proposed addition at the beginning of Section 4.3

Profiles for implementation should be selected through a reuse-first process: first map each DPI-H capability and interaction to existing international standards, IHE profiles, and other established implementation guides; identify only the residual unmet requirements; submit generalizable gaps to the relevant international development process; define a national extension only where a jurisdiction-specific requirement remains; and publish computable conformance artifacts and test plans for both the international core and the extension.
reviewer: Aaron Goldmuntz, IHE International, United States of America

sectionTitle: Services and Transactions: FHIR as the Recommended Framework
anchorNote: section 4.3.3 only
summary: Clarify the complementary roles of HL7 FHIR and IHE
text:
Clarify the complementary roles of HL7 FHIR and IHE

IHE strongly supports the draft's endorsement of HL7 FHIR as a recommended exchange framework. However, HL7 FHIR conformance alone does not define an end-to-end interoperable workflow. IHE profiles apply HL7 FHIR and other standards (e.g. DICOM, IEEE) to defined use cases, actors, transactions, options, and security dependencies. Section 4.3.3 should therefore direct countries first to existing globally governed HL7 FHIR implementation guides, like the IHE Profiles on HL7 FHIR are, and IHE profiles in general. Language should be avoided that could encourage independent national recreation of equivalent specifications. The guidance should also retain a practical transition path for mature, interoperable non-FHIR implementations and mixed environments.
suggestion:
Proposed addition to Section 4.3.3

HL7 FHIR should be treated as a foundational exchange standard, while IHE profiles and other implementation guides provide the use-case-level specification needed for interoperable workflows. Countries should adopt existing globally governed FHIR implementation guides, like HL7 FHIR based IHE profiles, wherever applicable rather than independently defining equivalent resources, terminologies, actors, operations, and transaction patterns. Any national profile should preserve a clearly identified international core and document only the additional national constraints or extensions.
reviewer: Aaron Goldmuntz, IHE International, United States of America

anchorNote: section 4.3.5 only
summary: Expand conformance into a full testing lifecycle
text:
Expand conformance into a full testing lifecycle

Section 4.3.5 should go beyond the creation of country-specific test beds. Countries should reuse international test plans, validators, simulators, reference data, and test-management tooling wherever possible. The lifecycle should include specification validation, developer self-testing, peer-to-peer multi-vendor interoperability testing, and, where required, formal conformity assessment. The guidance should distinguish these forms of evidence clearly: participation in an IHE Connectathon provides intensive implementation feedback and a baseline indication of profile conformance, while formal certification requires an authorized conformity assessment program.

For national extensions, the country should add only the tests required for the extension while retaining the international core test suite. Procurement should require transparent evidence tied to named profile versions, actors, options, and transactions rather than a broad, non-specific claim of standards compliance.
suggestion:
Proposed addition to Section 4.3.5

Countries should reuse established international test plans, validators, simulators, reference data, and test-management tooling, thereby also pooling the resources to establish and maintain these assets. Testing should progress from developer self-testing to multi-party interoperability testing and, where required, formal conformity assessment. National extensions should add tests for the extension while retaining the international core test suite. Procurement evidence should identify the exact profile version, actor, option, and transaction tested.
reviewer: Aaron Goldmuntz, IHE International, United States of America

text: Strengths: A major strength is that the guidance treats digital health infrastructure as more than a technical interoperability problem. Its attention to governance, responsible use of emerging technologies, trustworthy AI, and human oversight provides an important foundation for health systems that must remain safe, equitable, and accountable as AI capabilities become more deeply integrated into care and public health infrastructure.

anchorNote: placed on the section, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (medium): Asks to operationalise human oversight of AI; Ch.5 readiness/oversight section.
summary: Concerns / changes: I would encourage the guidance to operationalize meaningful human oversight more explicitly as a be…
text:
Concerns / changes: I would encourage the guidance to operationalize meaningful human oversight more explicitly as a behavioural and organizational capability, rather than primarily as the presence of a human reviewer. Effective oversight requires that people can detect potential errors, question AI recommendations, understand uncertainty, resist inappropriate deference, and meaningfully override or escalate decisions when necessary. Evaluation should therefore consider trust calibration, automation bias, perceived model authority, workload, and actual override behaviour, in addition to technical model performance.

For conversational and mental health related AI, I would also recommend attention to psychosocial risks that can affect human agency, including perceived empathy, emotional reliance, and excessive epistemic dependence on an AI system. These factors may influence whether users and professionals continue to exercise independent judgement even when formal human oversight mechanisms are present. Explicitly incorporating these behavioural dimensions would strengthen the guidance for high impact and vulnerable user contexts.

changeSets.title: Require effective, not nominal, human oversight of AI

text: The inclusion of meaningful human oversight and repeated evaluation is a major strength. text: LHR immutability should be reconciled with correction and legally required erasure. The LHR requires that records shall never be deleted, that previous versions remain retrievable, and that reconciliation actions are auditable. Elsewhere, the guidance recognises removal of erroneous records, data-subject rights, and deletion where legally required. The relationship between immutability, logical withdrawal, correction of wrong-person attribution and legally mandated erasure is therefore unclear.

Preserve immutable version history for ordinary clinical amendments where lawful, while distinguishing: (a) correction/amendment; (b) logical withdrawal or suppression; (c) controlled unlinking/reassignment of wrong-person data; and (d) legally mandated erasure. Specify how these actions propagate across federated nodes, replicas and backups while retaining only the audit evidence permitted by applicable law.

text: Offline/federated synchronisation needs minimum conflict-resolution semantics. However, 'reliable synchronisation' does not define the minimum semantics for concurrent clinically significant updates across offline or federated nodes. text: The architecture governs the stewardship of information models (SGI, LIMR) but does not standardise how models are made. Current artefact standards allow too many degrees of freedom: the same clinical concept can be modelled in many valid but incompatible ways, so two fully conformant implementations may still diverge semantically. A related, unnamed risk is the boundary problem: qualifiers, modifiers and localisations can be expressed in either the terminology or the information model, and this overlap breeds divergence.
suggestion: Require (in §3.4.5 and App. C) that artefacts in the LIMR be produced with a declared, uniform modelling method — one generic semantic pattern from which artefacts are derived by specialisation, with mandatory context (what, where, when, who, how, why) at capture — and test that meaning survives its application. The emerging CEN/ISO 13606 part 3 (SIAMM) work is one standards-track candidate; the requirement itself should remain method-neutral, preserving the draft's neutrality between modelling schools. Explicitly name — and assign governance responsibility for — the boundary problem between coding systems and information models.

text:
From: https://www.digitalhealth.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/csr-8169-health-connect-australia-architechture8.pdf: Australia offers a middle reference point. Not all interoperability capabilities should sit in a central ESB, and not all health specific capabilities should be pushed entirely to endpoints. Instead, it adopts an architecture in which nationally shared capabilities coexist with locally owned systems, with responsibilities distributed according to where they provide the greatest value – I feel this aligns with our current RA understanding as well.

Finally, one key lesson from ‘OpenHIE discussions with countries’ is that each box is often interpreted as requiring a separate systems or procurements, kicking off another debate. It might be useful to clarify that these DPI-H RA boxes represent reference capabilities and not target state, standalone platforms. Smaller or more centralised countries may choose to consolidate multiple capabilities within a single solution/platform/system and still achieve the intended outcomes.

anchorNote: quotation found in the text
summary: 1. The WHO Nomenclature Regulations, and the Member State obligations they create for mortality and morbidity reporting…
text:
1. The WHO Nomenclature Regulations, and the Member State obligations they create for mortality and morbidity reporting, are not referenced anywhere; the use of classifications is framed throughout as an elective national standards choice (p. 73).

2. The first health goal promises "population analytics including CRVS and mortality" (p. 22), yet the document contains no death certification or cause-of-death coding pathway — the phrase "cause of death" does not occur in its 254 pages.

3. A Required Terminology Service capability calls for the import of "local modifications of ICD and SNOMED CT" (TSF-1, p. 167). Modification of the international content is not permitted under either standard's licence and would undermine comparability; national extension and addition are the correct concepts.

4. ICHI does not appear in the document; ICF appears twice in passing; WHO-FIC once. The ICD-11 delivery infrastructure (API, coding tool), the annual update cycle, and the cost-free availability of the WHO classifications are not mentioned, while the licensing arrangements of other terminologies are described in some detail (pp. 20, 165, 171).

5. The AI chapter grounds trustworthy AI in governed terminology but does not consider knowledge-graph representations — the model on which the ICD-11 Foundation is built. The draft nowhere references the WHO Nomenclature Regulations or the Member State obligations they create — classification use is framed throughout as elective national standards selection. A floor for Member States should include the obligations Member States already stand on. TS requirement TSF-1 makes "local modifications of ICD and SNOMED CT" a Required import capability — something neither license permits, and which would compromise the statistical comparability the architecture promises. This is easily addressed with extension and national-addition language. Goal 1 promises "population analytics including CRVS and mortality," yet the document contains no death certification or cause-of-death coding pathway; the phrase "cause of death" does not occur in its 254 pages.

summary: I would like to suggest including illustrative use cases, which would also allow for examples from South America and ad…
text: I would like to suggest including illustrative use cases, which would also allow for examples from South America and add value to the document. For the section on National Implementations (page 83), I am sharing the case of Uruguay in two alternative versions for your consideration. DRAFT ENTRY A — Technical interoperability architecture emphasis Historia Clínica Electrónica Nacional (HCEN) is Uruguay's federated national longitudinal health record (LHR) and clinical-document exchange, developed and operated by the Salud.uy program of AGESIC (Agencia de Gobierno Electrónico y Sociedad de la Información y del Conocimiento) in conjunction with the Ministerio de Salud Pública. Architected as an IHE-based health information exchange rather than a central data store, the HCEN operates as a national interoperability node in which clinical documents remain in the custody of the institution that generated them while a central platform indexes and brokers their exchange in real time; its core components are the Índice Nacional de Usuarios de Salud, an Enterprise Master Patient Index implementing the IHE PIX/PDQ profiles for unique patient identification, the Registro Nacional de Documentos Clínicos (an IHE XDS.b document registry), a Bus de Salud (Enterprise Service Bus) serving as the single access point, a Sistema de Auditoría conformant to the IHE ATNA profile, and an Appliance/Conector Salud deployed at each provider that exposes the IHE XDS.b service interface. Each provider — both the public ASSE and the private mutualistas/IAMC of the Sistema Nacional Integrado de Salud (SNIS) — maintains its own institutional electronic record (HCE/HCD) and local document repository, generating standards-based electronic clinical documents (HL7 CDA R2, with HL7 v2 XML messaging, DICOM imaging, and the terminologies SNOMED CT including a Uruguayan national extension, LOINC and CIE-10) and registering each event's metadata in the national Registro de Eventos within 24 hours, enabling assembly of a longitudinal record across the country's mixed public-private landscape and exchange over the dedicated Red Salud network and AGESIC's Plataforma de Interoperabilidad (Interoperabilyty Platform). (https://www.gub.uy/agencia-gobierno-electronico-sociedad-informacion-conocimiento/historia-clinica-electronica-nacional). DRAFT ENTRY B — Governance/institutional and public-private SNIS continuity-of-care emphasis Historia Clínica Electrónica Nacional (HCEN) is Uruguay's nationally governed, federated longitudinal health record (LHR), conceived as the central instrument for continuity of care across the Sistema Nacional Integrado de Salud (SNIS), the country's universal mixed public-private health system. It is delivered by the Salud.uy program, launched in 2012 under an inter-institutional agreement among the Presidency of the Republic, the Ministerio de Salud Pública (MSP), the Ministerio de Economía y Finanzas (MEF) and AGESIC, which provides its institutional home and embeds it within Uruguay's broader digital-state infrastructure — the Plataforma de Gobierno Electrónico and its Plataforma de Interoperabilidad (PDI), the Red Salud private network, and the national digital identity used for citizen and professional authentication — with co-financing of roughly USD 21 million from the Inter-American Development Bank. Adopting a federated model that respects each institution's technological autonomy, the HCEN leaves clinical data in the custody of the public ASSE and the private mutualistas/IAMC that generated it while a state-operated central platform indexes events and brokers their secure, audited exchange, so that a user's information is available to any treating team regardless of provider or location; participation was made mandatory for all public and private providers by Decreto 242/017 (2017), with the adoption plan set by Ordenanza 1085/017, event-registration duties by Decreto 122/019, and provider incorporation by Ley 19.670, all operating within the data-protection guarantees of Ley 18.331 and a treatment-purposes consent model that is implied unless the patient opts out via the "Mi Historia Clínica Digital" citizen portal. Widely cited by the IDB and PAHO as one of Latin America's most advanced national digital-health systems — with 95% of the population holding at least one clinical document by end-2020 and more than 170 million documents registered by 2022 — the HCEN demonstrates how a national interoperability node can knit a fragmented public-private provider landscape into a single longitudinal record centered on the patient/user (https://www.gub.uy/agencia-gobierno-electronico-sociedad-informacion-conocimiento/historia-clinica-electronica-nacional)

text: Broad feedback: Align the approach more closely with the NHWA framework rather than focusing solely on registries. Health workforce data originate from multiple sources, including HR and payroll systems, professional registers, education systems, censuses, labour force surveys, and sources outside the health sector such as national statistical offices, ministries of finance and higher education, and private institutions. Adopt a comprehensive workforce perspective. The architecture should support data on workforce numbers, distribution, skills, education, inflows and outflows, employment, and future workforce needs—not only registration data. As emphasized in our NHWA training, priority challenges should guide how data are selected and organized. Strengthen the focus on data quality and multi-source integration. The role of triangulation(key to HWF data) should be made more explicit, highlighting the need to combine and validate information from different sources rather than relying on a single system. The architecture should also recognize the importance of analytical and evidence-generation capacities, involving HRH experts and analysts alongside IT specialists. Reinforce governance arrangements, particularly incentives and safeguards for data sharing and data privacy/confidentiality. Private-sector, military, and other stakeholders may require clear benefits, protections, sustainable financing, and differentiated access arrangements before they can contribute data and participate in the architecture. References: NHWA Handbook, [who.int/publications-detail-redirect/national-health-workforce-accounts-implementation-guide]NHWA implementation guide, HWF occupational mapping, HWF terminology

summary: Clarifying the Distinct and Complementary Roles of Core Terminology Standards The DPI-H draft correctly identifies SNOM…
text: Clarifying the Distinct and Complementary Roles of Core Terminology Standards The DPI-H draft correctly identifies SNOMED CT, ICD-11, and LOINC as open terminology standards forming the semantic foundation of the Terminology Service component. We welcome this recognition. However, the current text, in particular Section 3.4.5 and the REDDHI Open Standards list, groups these standards as equivalent alternatives without articulating their distinct clinical domains and governance structures. This framing may lead countries to conclude that implementing one standard fulfills the requirement for all, which would produce functionally incomplete national Terminology Services. We recommend the framework include a brief characterisation of each standard's primary clinical scope: ● SNOMED CT provides comprehensive clinical concept coverage: diagnoses, findings, procedures, body structures, substances, and more, enabling semantic interoperability across all domains of clinical care. It is maintained by SNOMED International, an independent not-for-profit standards development organisation operating under a national member model. ● ICD-11, maintained by WHO, is the international standard for mortality and morbidity statistics, disease classification, and reimbursement coding. It is a WHO product and is already mandated in many WHO Member States. ● LOINC, stewarded by the Regenstrief Institute, is the global standard for representing health observations, measurements, survey instruments and documents. Regenstrief Institute is a local, national and global leader dedicated to a world where better information empowers people to end disease and realize true health. ● UCUM stewarded by the Regenstrief Institute is the code system intended to include all units of measures being contemporarily used in international science, engineering, and business. ● HL7 FHIR® (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), published by HL7 International, is the prevailing API-based standard for health data exchange. It provides the technical architecture through which terminology standards are bound to clinical systems, including the FHIR Terminology Service specification referenced in DPI-H Section 3.4.5. We recommend Section 3.4.5 include a brief table or text passage illustrating how these standards operate together within a national Terminology Service deployment, rather than listing them as interchangeable alternatives. 2.
reviewer: SNOMED International; Regenstrief Institute; HL7 International, International

changeSets.title: Explain the complementary roles of SNOMED CT, ICD-11 and LOINC

anchorNote: placed on the section, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (high): About SGI and the NRC model reference in §3.4.5.
summary: Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) — A Joint Partnership Offer The DPI-H framework introduces Semantic Governance…
text: Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) — A Joint Partnership Offer The DPI-H framework introduces Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI) as a new national-level governance architecture and, notably, cites SNOMED International's National Release Center (NRC) model as one of the only tested frameworks for SGI implementation. We commend this recognition of the NRC model as a proven reference. The current text, however, describes SGI as a national responsibility without establishing a formal relationship between national SGI bodies and the international standards organisations that develop and maintain the underlying terminologies. This creates a governance gap: countries may establish SGI processes independently, leading to fragmentation, duplicated effort, and in the absence of international guidance semantic divergence across national implementations. SNOMED International and Regenstrief collectively offer to serve as formal International SGI Reference Partners to WHO and ITU. In practice, this would mean: ● SNOMED International: providing National Release Centre (NRC) governance templates, Snowstorm (open-source FHIR Terminology Server), SNOMED CT Browser, and training resources to countries establishing SGI bodies aligned to the NRC model. ● Regenstrief Institute: providing a LOINC Terminology FHIR Service, with resources that include code system, value set, concept map and questionnaire. Regenstrief also provides LOINC Panels and Forms,UCUM specifications and education and training guidance and laboratory for countries establishing national observation and units of measure catalogues within their SGI. We propose that the DPI-H framework explicitly recognise our two organisations as reference implementation partners for SGI, and that WHO/ITU establish a formal Technical Advisory Group comprising representatives of SNOMED International, Regenstrief Institute, the WHO, and additional Standards Development Organization participation, such as HL7 International, to develop SGI implementation guidance for national programmes. 3.
reviewer: SNOMED International; Regenstrief Institute; HL7 International, International

changeSets.title: Present terminology governance as federated with international SDOs

sectionTitle: Conformance and Testing across Architecture and Components
anchorNote: placed on the section, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (medium): Cites Section 3.7 conformance; offers FHIR terminology testing framework.
summary: FHIR Terminology Conformance: A Ready-Made Testing Framework Section 3.7 of the DPI-H draft describes a testable, machi…
text: FHIR Terminology Conformance: A Ready-Made Testing Framework Section 3.7 of the DPI-H draft describes a testable, machine-readable architecture in which national implementations are verified against published conformance profiles. This is precisely the architecture that the HL7 FHIR Terminology Service specification was designed to support. SNOMED International and Regenstrief Institute acknowledge and support that HL7 International has published a mature FHIR Terminology Service capability model, including operations for CodeSystem lookup, ValueSet expansion, and concept translation, each of which maps directly to the DPI-H Terminology Service functions described in Section 3.4.5. Additionally, SNOMED International's Snowstorm server and Regenstrief's LOINC FHIR Terminology Service both implement this specification and are available as open-source reference implementations. We recommend that: ● The DPI-H conformance framework (Section 3.7) explicitly reference the HL7 FHIR Terminology Service specification (HL7 FHIR R4/R5, http://hl7.org/fhir/terminology-service.html) as the baseline conformance model for national Terminology Service implementations. ● We recommend that the organizations be invited to jointly develop a DPI-H Terminology Service Conformance Profile that countries can use to verify their implementations against the DPI-H standard. ● WHO/ITU consider an open reference implementation programme, in which nationally deployed instances of Snowstorm (SNOMED CT) and the LOINC FHIR API are certified as conformant reference implementations. 4.
reviewer: SNOMED International; Regenstrief Institute; HL7 International, International

changeSets.title: Govern adapters and transformations that may alter meaning

anchorNote: placed on the section, by a placement agent reading the comment against the text (medium): Licensing/open access for the Terminology Service requirement.
summary: Open Access for Low- and Middle-Income Countries DPI-H is explicitly designed to support countries at all stages of dig…
text: Open Access for Low- and Middle-Income Countries DPI-H is explicitly designed to support countries at all stages of digital health maturity, with particular focus on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The framework's Terminology Service requirement must therefore be achievable without prohibitive licensing costs. We note that an open access pathway already exists across our two organisations' standards, and we recommend that the DPI-H framework make this explicit: ● SNOMED International's SNOMED CT Global Patient Set (GPS) is freely available to all countries regardless of membership status, providing a clinically curated subset of SNOMED CT for use in LMIC settings without licensing cost. Corrections on inaccurately stated GPS information within the DPI-H will be submitted in the formal SNOMED International individual response. ● LOINC is available at no charge under an open license, It is available for use in commercial and non-commercial in accordance with terms of use provisions. ● UCUM is available at no charge under an open license available for use in commercial and non-commercial in accordance with terms of use provisions. We recommend Section 3.4.5 and the REDDHI Open Standards annex include explicit reference to the GPS as the LMIC-accessible entry point for SNOMED CT, and that the Licensing footnote (currently footnote 47 in the draft) be expanded to articulate the full open access pathway across SNOMED CT and LOINC. Conclusion Regenstrief and SNOMED International steward terminology and interoperability standards collectively used in over 80 countries and deployed in hundreds of millions of patient records worldwide. We have each independently arrived at a shared conviction: the DPI-H framework is a significant and timely contribution to global health informatics, and it deserves a robust, internationally coordinated implementation architecture. In this letter, we do not write to advocate for the interests of any single organisation. We write to offer the collective technical capacity of the global health standards community, freely and in partnership, to help WHO and ITU translate this ambitious framework into working national infrastructure. We would welcome the opportunity to meet with the DPI-H technical team at a mutually convenient time to discuss this response in depth, and we stand ready to contribute to any joint technical working group WHO and ITU may convene. text: §3.6 already provides shared data exchange — distributed mediation, eventing, a participant registry — and we support it. What no component owns is following a commitment through: tracking whether a referral was actioned, noticing the follow-up that never happens, closing the loop. §3.6.1 lists "orchestrating a multi-step transaction" among the mediation functions, but that routes one exchange in flight — not a commitment's lifecycle across time: a referral (accepted → attended → outcome, or the follow-up that never comes) or a claim (eligibility → pre-auth → settlement, or the claim that stalls). Goal 3 asks for exactly this ("coordinate care over time… while tracking adherence and quality"), but the draft folds it into the CDSE and into "care-coordination and referral tools" outside DPI-H. We recommend recognising this as a shared capability, distinct from decision support. The §2.1.1 test for shared infrastructure — reusable, stable interface, no lock-in, foundational not programme-specific — is met by it. We mean the shared exchange between systems — not every consuming application (an EMR or a payroll system is rightly application-layer). (On whether such a capability may be transactional, see C2.) It makes breaks in continuity visible; it does not assume the digital layer can resolve the underlying service-delivery constraint — a vacancy, or a lack of capacity — and it should be designed for real conditions: intermittent connectivity, workforce gaps, weak supervision, and incomplete facility-capability information.

changeSets.title: Address closing the loop on clinical workflows across systems

anchorNote: section 3.1 only

text: Box 3.1 requires DPI-H components to be "non-transactional… not point-of-care workflow engines or clinical transaction processors." The concern is sound — shared infrastructure should not concentrate control, or make its operator accountable for clinical or financial decisions(§3.6.3) — but the rule is too broad. The draft's own foundational example, payments DPI ("rails for moving money securely and at scale between parties", §1.2.3), is transactional and is bedrock public infrastructure; it meets the concern by keeping settlement and balances with the banks. A coordination or claims fabric (C1, C3) works the same way — it carries the transaction and keeps processing and authoritative decisions with the participants. The draft's own architecture already contains a stateful, lifecycle-tracking DPI-H component: the Public Health Surveillance Platform does "case registration and management… outcome tracking" and contact "follow-up" — so the criterion is not even applied consistently within DPI-H today. We recommend refining the criterion: a DPI-H component may carry transactions provided it keeps processing and control with the participants rather than concentrating them. The other Box 3.1 tests — shared, reusable, publicly governed, open, technology-neutral — continue to hold the boundary.
reviewer: CoWEAVE - Medtronic LABS; eGov Foundation; Open Healthcare Network Foundation, International

anchorNote: quotation found in the text

text: The same pattern in financing. The draft says "only one genuinely new DPI-H component emerges from the financing analysis: the Benefits Package Registry," and its appendix places the Contract & Benefits Management System — which "processes claims and contributions" — explicitly outside DPI-H, as a "functional application." We agree the processing belongs there. suggestion:
Insert complete worked-example box; retain blood-pressure example: Worked example: an ICD-11-coded clinical diagnosis

A clinician records a diagnosis using ICD-11 terminology. The terminology service resolves the selected concept against the specified WHO release and provides its identifier, title, relevant properties, and available coding instructions. For example, the WHO API documentation identifies cholera by Foundation URI http://id.who.int/icd/entity/257068234; its MMS category code is 1A00. The Foundation URI and the MMS code are recorded with their respective namespace and release, rather than treated as the same identifier.

The LIMR defines the clinical statement: whose condition it is, the encounter, onset or relevant time, clinical and verification status, and other context required for the use case. The record preserves the clinician's statement and any valid coded expression, including linked postcoordination detail when applicable.

A receiving clinical system interprets the diagnosis using the same identified ICD-11 content. A statistical process derives the applicable MMS representation and applies the relevant selection and aggregation rules, retaining a link to the source statement. No conversion to SNOMED CT is a prerequisite for this path. Where another system requires a different terminology, any additional mapping is governed separately, with its limitations recorded.

text: Central ICD-11 terminology and classification pathway — The main correction presents ICD-11 as a primary clinical terminology and statistical classification, with continuity into reporting. The legal paragraph incorporates reviewer A07.02 with corrected instruments and scope: WHO Constitution, Articles 2(s), 21(b), 22 and 64 (https://apps.who.int/gb/bd/pdf_files/BD_49th-en.pdf); WHO Nomenclature Regulations 1967 (https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/who-nomenclature-regulations-1967); WHA72.15 (https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA72/A72_R15-en.pdf); WHA54.21 (https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA54/ea54r21.pdf). It omits the unsupported 2023 amendment claim. Clinical capabilities: WHO clinical documentation hub (https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/clinician-documentation-hub) and WHO ICD API data model (https://icd.who.int/docs/icd-api/APIDoc-Version2/). The supplied data-continuity discussion paper supports the design proposal but is not an adopted WHO position.
suggestion:
Replace one existing paragraph with all four proposed paragraphs, in this order: Health content standards supply the shared meaning and structure on which interoperability depends. The architecture distinguishes exchange and information-model standards from clinical terminology, statistical classification, measurement identifiers, and product identification. HL7 FHIR provides an exchange-oriented representation; ICD-11 provides both clinical terminology and statistical classification; ICF addresses functioning and disability; and ICHI addresses health interventions. SNOMED CT, LOINC, GS1 and IDMP-family identifiers, DICOM, IHE profiles, and specifications such as the International Patient Summary serve their respective purposes. These standards are selected and combined according to the information and functions required.

ICD-11 is a viable primary semantic standard for clinical information within its scope. It provides a Foundation of identified concepts, multilingual terminology, a statistical linearization for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics, and rules for adding detail through postcoordination. Systems may capture clinical information directly in ICD-11, exchange the identified concepts and valid expressions, and reuse that information for reporting under the applicable classification rules. Implementing this route does not depend on first recording or converting the information into SNOMED CT.

The original clinical statement, its precise identifiers and coded expression, and its context should remain available when a statistical category or other derived representation is produced. A statistical grouping is not a substitute for the more detailed source meaning. Additional standards remain necessary for data outside the selected terminology's scope and for such functions as laboratory measurement, units, medicinal-product identification, imaging, and exchange structure. Countries should publish their selected profiles and demonstrate semantic preservation through conformance tests.

National standards selection should distinguish clinical implementation choices from international statistical obligations. Articles 21(b) and 22 of the WHO Constitution provide for Health Assembly regulations on disease, cause-of-death and public-health nomenclatures, with entry into force subject to the prescribed rejection and reservation procedures. The WHO Nomenclature Regulations 1967 establish ICD-based mortality and morbidity statistics, annual cause-of-death statistics, medical certification and provision of statistics to WHO within their stated scope. WHA72.15 adopted ICD-11 with effect from 1 January 2022, subject to transitional arrangements that accommodate continued reporting with earlier revisions. Architecture should therefore preserve the applicable ICD statistical reporting pathway from clinical documentation and death certification through coding to reported results. ICF was endorsed by WHA54.21 for use as appropriate; ICHI addresses interventions within WHO's nomenclature mandate. These classifications have distinct roles and legal status. Their inclusion in WHO-FIC does not itself place all three under identical reporting obligations or require them in every clinical field.
